cardiac-arrest-als.mechanism: **Disorganised electrical activity** stops effective pumping so **coronary perfusion** and **cerebral oxygen delivery** cease within seconds.
cardiac-arrest-als.manifestation: **Sudden collapse** with **pulselessness** and agonal breathing progresses rapidly to **unresponsiveness** if untreated.
cardiac-arrest-als.intervention: **Chest compressions** with **defibrillation** for shockable rhythms plus **adrenaline** and correction of reversible causes restores circulation.
cardiac-arrest-als.adverse: **Chest compressions** can fracture **ribs** and injure **lung tissue** through forceful sternal pressure on the thorax.

cardiac-conduction-ecg.trigger: The normal heartbeat starts when the **sinoatrial node** fires spontaneously in response to autonomic and metabolic demand. Disease of the node or **conduction tissue** can interrupt or disorder this impulse.
cardiac-conduction-ecg.target: The impulse spreads through atria, pauses at the **atrioventricular node**, then travels rapidly through the **His Purkinje system**. This sequence coordinates atrial then ventricular contraction.
cardiac-conduction-ecg.mechanism: Atrial depolarisation gives the **P wave**, ventricular depolarisation gives the **QRS complex**, and repolarisation gives the **T wave**. Block delays or drops ventricular activation, while atrial fibrillation makes activation chaotic.
cardiac-conduction-ecg.manifestation: Conduction block can cause **bradycardia**, dizziness and **syncope** from low output. **Atrial fibrillation** causes an irregular pulse and increases stroke risk from atrial stasis and clot.
cardiac-conduction-ecg.intervention: A **pacemaker** replaces failed impulse generation or conduction in symptomatic block. An **anticoagulant** reduces clot formation and **stroke** in atrial fibrillation but does not correct the rhythm itself.
cardiac-conduction-ecg.adverse: A **pacemaker** can cause infection, lead displacement or pacing induced heart dysfunction. An **anticoagulant** increases **bleeding**, including gastrointestinal and intracranial bleeding, by impairing clot formation.

cardiac-cycle-pv-loop.trigger: Venous return filling the **left ventricle** during diastole creates the physiological demand for ejection against **aortic pressure**.
cardiac-cycle-pv-loop.target: **Ventricular myocardium**, **mitral valve** and **aortic valve** determine filling, pressure generation and ejection in sequence.
cardiac-cycle-pv-loop.mechanism: Rising ventricular pressure closes the **mitral valve**, then opens the **aortic valve** for ejection, while relaxation and filling reset **stroke volume** on the loop.
cardiac-cycle-pv-loop.manifestation: Valve closure produces **heart sounds**, ejection determines **stroke volume**, and increased preload, afterload or contractility widens, raises or shifts the **pressure volume loop**.
cardiac-cycle-pv-loop.intervention: An **inotrope** increases **contractility**, shifting the loop upward and leftward with greater ejection for the same filling.
cardiac-cycle-pv-loop.adverse: That same increased **contractility** raises myocardial oxygen demand, so an **inotrope** can provoke **arrhythmia** and ischaemia in a vulnerable heart.

cardiac-inotropes.trigger: Heart failure with weak **contractility** and low output, often with heightened **sympathetic drive**, creates the need for inotropic support.
cardiac-inotropes.target: **Na/K ATPase**, **beta1 receptors** and **phosphodiesterase 3** in cardiac myocytes control intracellular calcium and therefore force of contraction.
cardiac-inotropes.mechanism: Pump blockade raises intracellular sodium and calcium, beta1 activation raises **cAMP** and calcium entry, and PDE3 inhibition prevents **cAMP** breakdown, all increasing calcium for contraction.
cardiac-inotropes.manifestation: Weak contraction explains **breathlessness**, fatigue and **pulmonary oedema** from low output and raised filling pressures, improving when contractility rises.
cardiac-inotropes.intervention: **Digoxin** blocks Na/K ATPase, **dobutamine** stimulates beta1 receptors, and **milrinone** inhibits phosphodiesterase 3 to strengthen contraction and dilate vessels.
cardiac-inotropes.adverse: Digoxin causes **arrhythmia**, nausea and visual disturbance, dobutamine causes tachycardia and arrhythmia, and milrinone causes **hypotension** and arrhythmia from vasodilation and raised cAMP.

cardiac-output-frank-starling.trigger: Increased **venous return** or metabolic demand requires greater **cardiac output** to maintain tissue perfusion.
cardiac-output-frank-starling.target: **Ventricular filling**, **myocardial contractility** and **afterload** determine stroke volume in the Frank Starling relationship.
cardiac-output-frank-starling.mechanism: Greater stretch optimises **actin myosin overlap** and calcium sensitivity, so the ventricle ejects a larger **stroke volume** until overstretch or failure flattens the curve.
cardiac-output-frank-starling.manifestation: Rising output prevents **pulmonary congestion** when filling increases, while a flattened failing curve causes breathlessness, oedema and low **cardiac output**.
cardiac-output-frank-starling.intervention: A **positive inotrope** shifts the curve upward, a **diuretic** moves the point left by reducing preload, and a **vasodilator** reduces afterload.
cardiac-output-frank-starling.adverse: A **diuretic** causing excessive volume loss reduces **preload** and cardiac output, producing hypotension and **acute kidney injury**.

cardiac-tamponade.trigger: Rapid bleeding, inflammation, malignancy or trauma fills the **pericardial sac** with **fluid** or blood faster than it can stretch.
cardiac-tamponade.target: Rising pressure in the relatively stiff **pericardium** compresses all cardiac chambers, especially the thin walled **right atrium** and right ventricle.
cardiac-tamponade.mechanism: Compression limits diastolic filling and equalises chamber pressures, so **stroke volume** and **cardiac output** fall despite compensatory tachycardia.
cardiac-tamponade.manifestation: The **Beck triad** of hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure and muffled heart sounds, with **pulsus paradoxus**, reflects impaired filling and output.
cardiac-tamponade.intervention: **Pericardiocentesis** or **surgical drainage** removes pericardial fluid and relieves compression, while intravenous fluids give temporary support before definitive drainage.
cardiac-tamponade.adverse: **Pericardiocentesis** can injure myocardium, coronary vessels or lung, and fluids alone can worsen congestion without relieving the underlying **pericardial pressure**.

cardiomyopathies.trigger: Genetic variants, alcohol, viral injury, infiltration or deposition disease act as triggers that remodel the **ventricular myocardium** and impair **cardiac muscle** function.
cardiomyopathies.target: Disease affects **cardiomyocytes**, sarcomeres and the **extracellular matrix**, producing dilated, hypertrophic or restrictive patterns of the **left ventricle**.
cardiomyopathies.mechanism: Dilated ventricles develop **systolic failure**, hypertrophied walls develop **diastolic dysfunction** and dynamic **outflow obstruction**, and restrictive walls resist filling.
cardiomyopathies.manifestation: Patients develop **breathlessness** and **oedema**, chest pain, palpitations and syncope from low output, congestion, arrhythmia and raised filling pressures.
cardiomyopathies.intervention: **Heart failure therapy** reduces load and harmful neurohormonal activation, while **treating the cause** removes alcohol, iron, amyloid or other drivers.
cardiomyopathies.adverse: Heart failure drugs can cause **hypotension**, **bradycardia**, kidney injury and **hyperkalaemia** through vasodilation and reduced aldosterone or sympathetic action.

cell-injury-necrosis.trigger: **Hypoxia** from **ischaemia**, toxins or infection reduces oxygen delivery and initiates reversible injury that progresses if the insult persists.
cell-injury-necrosis.target: Mitochondrial **oxidative phosphorylation** fails first, depleting cellular **ATP** needed for membrane pumps and synthetic processes.
cell-injury-necrosis.mechanism: ATP loss disables the **sodium potassium pump**, causing sodium and water influx, cell swelling, **calcium** entry and eventual **membrane rupture**.
cell-injury-necrosis.manifestation: Irreversible injury produces **necrosis** with inflammation, and its pattern varies as coagulative in most solid tissues, liquefactive in **brain** and caseous in **tuberculosis**.
cell-injury-necrosis.intervention: Restoring **oxygen** and blood flow early can salvage reversible injury, while **antioxidants** aim to limit reactive oxygen mediated damage.
cell-injury-necrosis.adverse: Reperfusion after **ischaemia** can paradoxically worsen injury through **reactive oxygen species**, calcium overload and inflammatory recruitment.

cell-wall-antibiotics.trigger: Actively growing **bacteria** must build and remodel **peptidoglycan** to survive, making wall synthesis a selective target.
cell-wall-antibiotics.target: Drugs act on cytoplasmic precursor steps, the **lipid carrier**, **D Ala D Ala** ends or **penicillin binding proteins** that cross link the wall.
cell-wall-antibiotics.mechanism: Precursors are carried across the membrane as **Lipid II**, **glycan chains** grow, and **transpeptidases** cross link them. Blocking any step leaves a weak wall that swells and lyses.
cell-wall-antibiotics.manifestation: Effective treatment resolves **fever** and local signs as **bacterial lysis** and immune clearance reduce the load. Failure suggests resistance, poor penetration or an organism without the target wall structure.
cell-wall-antibiotics.intervention: **Beta lactams** bind penicillin binding proteins, **vancomycin** binds D Ala D Ala, and fosfomycin or bacitracin block earlier steps. Beta lactamase inhibitors protect partner beta lactams from bacterial enzymes.
cell-wall-antibiotics.adverse: **Beta lactams** can cause allergy, including anaphylaxis, and seizures when they accumulate. **Vancomycin** can injure the kidney and cause infusion related flushing.

central-sympatholytics-pressors.trigger: High **sympathetic tone** sustaining hypertension, or shock with inadequate vascular tone and **hypotension**, requires tone to be lowered centrally or raised at vessels.
central-sympatholytics-pressors.target: Central drugs stimulate brainstem **alpha-2 receptors** to cut sympathetic outflow, while noradrenaline stimulates vascular **alpha-1 receptors** and cardiac **beta-1 receptors**.
central-sympatholytics-pressors.mechanism: Alpha-2 stimulation reduces **noradrenaline release** and sympathetic outflow, methyldopa forms a false transmitter with the same effect, and alpha-1 stimulation contracts **vascular smooth muscle**.
central-sympatholytics-pressors.manifestation: Excess outflow explains raised **blood pressure** and heart rate, while loss of vascular tone explains **shock** with poor organ perfusion despite fluid filling.
central-sympatholytics-pressors.intervention: **Clonidine** stimulates central alpha-2 receptors, **methyldopa** reduces central sympathetic outflow, and **noradrenaline** constricts vessels to restore pressure in shock.
central-sympatholytics-pressors.adverse: Central alpha-2 stimulation causes **sedation** and dry mouth with **rebound hypertension** on sudden withdrawal, while noradrenaline can cause **arrhythmias** and tissue injury from extravasation.

cervical-cancer-hpv.trigger: Persistent high risk **HPV infection** at the **transformation zone** initiates malignant change in susceptible epithelium.
cervical-cancer-hpv.target: Targets are cervical **squamous cells** plus growth controls **p53** and **Rb protein** that normally restrain division.
cervical-cancer-hpv.mechanism: Viral **E6** and **E7** proteins block **p53** and Rb control so infected cells proliferate through CIN toward invasion.
cervical-cancer-hpv.manifestation: Early **CIN** is silent on **screening** while invasion causes postcoital **bleeding**, discharge and pelvic spread.
cervical-cancer-hpv.intervention: **Vaccination** prevents HPV infection while **LEEP excision** removes CIN and **chemoradiation** treats invasive disease.
cervical-cancer-hpv.adverse: **LEEP** can cause bleeding and cervical **stenosis** with preterm birth risk while **chemoradiation** injures bowel and bladder.

chelating-agents.trigger: Excess **iron**, **heavy metals** such as lead and mercury, or **copper** accumulation in Wilson disease creates a toxic metal burden.
chelating-agents.target: Chelators bind free and tissue **iron**, **lead** and other heavy metals, or **copper**, forming stable complexes for excretion.
chelating-agents.mechanism: The drug donates binding groups that surround the **metal ion**, prevent it generating **free radicals** or binding enzymes, and form a soluble **chelate complex**.
chelating-agents.manifestation: Iron overload injures **heart**, **liver** and endocrine glands, lead injures brain, kidney and marrow, and copper injures liver and **basal ganglia**.
chelating-agents.intervention: **Desferrioxamine** chelates **iron**, **penicillamine** chelates **copper**, and succimer or dimercaprol chelates lead and other heavy metals.
chelating-agents.adverse: Chelators can cause **renal injury**, **hypotension** with rapid infusion, visual or auditory toxicity with iron chelators, and **myelosuppression** or rash with penicillamine.

chemotherapy-supportive-drugs.trigger: Chemotherapy injures normal tissues while killing tumour cells, causing **folate depletion**, bladder injury, uric acid release and **neutropenia**.
chemotherapy-supportive-drugs.target: **Folate pathways** in normal cells, **acrolein** in urine, **uric acid** from tumour breakdown and the **G-CSF receptor** on marrow precursors are the protective targets.
chemotherapy-supportive-drugs.mechanism: **Methotrexate** blocks folate activation in normal cells, cyclophosphamide releases **acrolein** that irritates bladder, tumour lysis releases uric acid, and marrow suppression lowers neutrophil production.
chemotherapy-supportive-drugs.manifestation: This explains **mucositis** and marrow injury from folate block, **haemorrhagic cystitis** from acrolein, kidney injury from uric acid and infection risk from neutropenia.
chemotherapy-supportive-drugs.intervention: **Leucovorin** rescues folate depleted normal cells, **mesna** neutralises acrolein in urine, **rasburicase** breaks down uric acid, and **filgrastim** stimulates neutrophil production.
chemotherapy-supportive-drugs.adverse: Leucovorin can rescue tumour cells if mistimed, mesna causes **nausea** and rash, rasburicase causes **haemolysis** in susceptible patients, and filgrastim causes bone pain and splenic enlargement.

cholera.trigger: Ingested **Vibrio cholerae** from contaminated water colonises the small bowel and secretes **cholera toxin** without invading the mucosa.
cholera.target: Toxin permanently activates **adenylyl cyclase** in enterocytes, raising cyclic AMP and opening the **CFTR chloride channel** on the luminal membrane.
cholera.mechanism: **Chloride secretion** into the lumen draws sodium and water passively, producing profuse **secretory diarrhoea** that overwhelms colonic absorption.
cholera.manifestation: **Rice water stool**, vomiting and rapid dehydration cause sunken eyes, poor skin turgor, **hypovolaemic shock** and metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate loss.
cholera.intervention: **Oral rehydration solution** uses glucose coupled sodium absorption to replace losses, **intravenous fluids** restore circulation in severe disease, and antibiotics shorten excretion.
cholera.adverse: Inadequate replacement allows worsening **shock** and kidney injury, excess rapid fluids can cause overload, and **antibiotics** can cause gastrointestinal upset and resistance.

chronic-inflammation-granuloma.trigger: A **persistent trigger** such as retained microbes, autoantigen or foreign material refuses clearance. Failed acute resolution keeps **immune activation** switched on.
chronic-inflammation-granuloma.target: Tissue **macrophages**, recruited **lymphocytes** and repairing **fibroblasts** are the targets. Nearby **blood vessels** grow and feed the inflamed site.
chronic-inflammation-granuloma.mechanism: **Interferon gamma** plus **tumour necrosis factor** and interleukin 17 activate macrophages. Fused cells form **granuloma** while fibroblasts lay down **fibrosis**.
chronic-inflammation-granuloma.manifestation: Ongoing injury causes chronic **tissue swelling** with pain and lost function. Healing by **fibrosis** stiffens organs while **granuloma** nodules mark the biopsy.
chronic-inflammation-granuloma.intervention: **Removing the trigger** cures disease when the cause can go. Persistent cases need **anti-inflammatory** drugs while targeted **anti-cytokine biologic** therapy blocks key signals.
chronic-inflammation-granuloma.adverse: **Anti-cytokine biologic** therapy damps host defence so **latent infection** can reactivate. Broad **immunosuppression** also raises infection and impairs wound healing.

chronic-kidney-disease.trigger: Diabetes and hypertension cause progressive **glomerular injury** and **nephron loss** over months to years.
chronic-kidney-disease.target: Remaining nephrons undergo **glomerular hyperfiltration**, while **tubulointerstitial fibrosis** reduces filtration, endocrine and excretory kidney functions.
chronic-kidney-disease.mechanism: Falling **glomerular filtration** retains urea, potassium, acid and phosphate, and reduces **erythropoietin** and active vitamin D production.
chronic-kidney-disease.manifestation: Retention and hormone failure cause **anaemia**, fluid overload, hypertension and **mineral bone disorder** with vascular calcification risk.
chronic-kidney-disease.intervention: **Blood pressure control** with renin angiotensin blockade slows progression, **phosphate binders** and vitamin D treat mineral disorder, and **dialysis** replaces filtration.
chronic-kidney-disease.adverse: **Renin angiotensin blockers** can cause hyperkalaemia and a fall in filtration, while **erythropoietin** therapy may raise blood pressure and thrombotic risk.

chronic-pancreatitis.trigger: Repeated **alcohol injury** plus smoking and **genetic susceptibility** start the damage. Recurrent **acute pancreatitis** attacks keep scarring an already vulnerable gland.
chronic-pancreatitis.target: Digestive **acinar cells**, insulin making **islet cells** and draining **pancreatic ducts** are targets. Surrounding **stromal tissue** scars around them.
chronic-pancreatitis.mechanism: Repeated necrosis heals by **fibrosis** that strangulates ducts into stones and **duct obstruction**. Lost acini and islets end enzyme and **insulin secretion**.
chronic-pancreatitis.manifestation: Lost enzymes cause fatty **steatorrhoea** with bloating and **weight loss**. Lost islets cause **diabetes** while strictures sustain chronic **abdominal pain**.
chronic-pancreatitis.intervention: **Enzyme replacement** with meals restores digestion and weight while **alcohol abstinence** halts injury. **Endoscopic or surgical drainage** relieves blocked ducts and eases pain.
chronic-pancreatitis.adverse: **Enzyme replacement** in excess causes nausea and **abdominal cramps** from luminal load. Strong **pain control** with opioids brings constipation and dependence that complicate care.

cml-philadelphia.trigger: Reciprocal swap fusing the **BCR gene** with the **ABL gene** in a **haemopoietic stem cell** creates the Philadelphia chromosome. The abnormal clone gains a lasting growth advantage.
cml-philadelphia.target: The fusion **tyrosine kinase** stays switched on inside **myeloid stem cells** and drives excess **granulocyte** production.
cml-philadelphia.mechanism: The kinase phosphorylates downstream **growth pathways** without normal control, so **myeloid precursors** divide and survive excessively. Maturation is preserved early, so **blasts** remain low.
cml-philadelphia.manifestation: Excess **granulocytes** crowd the blood and **spleen**, causing **splenomegaly** with fatigue in the chronic phase. Later **blast** expansion marks accelerated and blast phases.
cml-philadelphia.intervention: **Tyrosine kinase inhibitor** therapy blocks the **BCR-ABL kinase** pocket and restores controlled maturation. **Stem cell transplant** can replace the diseased clone in advanced disease.
cml-philadelphia.adverse: **Tyrosine kinase inhibitor** drugs also suppress normal **marrow**, causing **cytopenias** with fatigue. Fluid retention with **periorbital oedema** follows off target kinase effects.

coagulation-dic.trigger: Local vessel injury exposes **collagen** and **tissue factor**, starting a contained clot. In DIC a systemic trigger such as sepsis or malignancy activates clotting throughout the circulation.
coagulation-dic.target: Primary haemostasis uses **platelets** and **von Willebrand factor**, while secondary haemostasis uses clotting factors that generate **thrombin**. Thrombin converts fibrinogen into stabilising fibrin.
coagulation-dic.mechanism: Platelets form a plug, then the cascade produces **thrombin** and a cross linked **fibrin** mesh, later removed by **plasmin** in fibrinolysis. In DIC widespread fibrin consumes platelets and factors faster than they are replaced.
coagulation-dic.manifestation: A local clot stops bleeding, but DIC causes simultaneous **thrombosis** in small vessels and **bleeding** from consumed factors. This produces oozing, purpura, **organ failure** and confusion.
coagulation-dic.intervention: DIC treatment targets the underlying **cause**, such as sepsis, while replacing consumed **platelets**, plasma factors or fibrinogen when bleeding. **Heparin** is reserved for thrombosis dominant cases under specialist care.
coagulation-dic.adverse: Blood component replacement can cause **transfusion reactions** and circulatory overload. **Heparin** can worsen **bleeding** in DIC because it further impairs an already depleted clotting system.

coeliac-malabsorption.trigger: Dietary **gluten intake** with gliadin peptides starts disease in susceptible people. Carrying **HLA DQ2** or **HLA DQ8** risk genes permits the response.
coeliac-malabsorption.target: Small bowel **enterocytes** on villi, lamina propria **CD4 T cells** and modifying **tissue transglutaminase** are the targets.
coeliac-malabsorption.mechanism: Deamidated **gliadin** presented by **HLA DQ2** activates lamina propria **CD4 T cells**. Cytokine injury then flattens villi into **villous atrophy** with poor absorption.
coeliac-malabsorption.manifestation: Flat mucosa causes **malabsorption** with diarrhoea, bloating and weight loss. Poor uptake also causes **iron deficiency** anaemia and weak bone from low **vitamin D**.
coeliac-malabsorption.intervention: Strict **gluten free diet** removes antigen and lets villi regrow. Added **dietitian support** plus **vitamin replacement** corrects anaemia and bone deficits.
coeliac-malabsorption.adverse: Ongoing gluten exposure risks **osteoporosis** with fractures from chronic calcium loss. Poorly planned diet without help can cause added **nutrient deficiency** despite healing.

complement-system.trigger: Antibody bound microbes activate the **classical pathway**, microbial sugars activate the **lectin pathway**, and spontaneous C3 tickover drives the **alternative pathway**.
complement-system.target: All pathways converge on **C3 convertase**, which cleaves **C3** and amplifies complement activation on microbial surfaces.
complement-system.mechanism: C3 cleavage deposits **C3b** for opsonisation, releases **C5a** for chemotaxis and initiates the **membrane attack complex** that lyses susceptible cells.
complement-system.manifestation: Efficient complement supports microbial clearance, whereas **complement deficiency** predisposes to recurrent **encapsulated bacterial infection** and uncontrolled activation causes tissue inflammation.
complement-system.intervention: A **C5 blocker** prevents membrane attack complex formation in complement mediated disease, and replacing a missing **complement component** restores host defence where feasible.
complement-system.adverse: Blocking **C5** impairs killing of **Neisseria**, increasing meningococcal infection risk despite vaccination and requiring vigilance for sepsis.

congenital-heart-shunts.trigger: A congenital defect such as an **atrial septal defect**, **ventricular septal defect** or persistent **ductus arteriosus** connects the two circulations.
congenital-heart-shunts.target: The defect shunts blood between **atria**, **ventricles** or great arteries, depending on the pressure difference across the opening.
congenital-heart-shunts.mechanism: Higher left sided pressure drives **left to right shunt** and pulmonary overcirculation, but chronic pressure can reverse flow in **Eisenmenger syndrome**.
congenital-heart-shunts.manifestation: Left to right shunts cause breathlessness, poor growth and pulmonary hypertension, while reversed shunting or **tetralogy of Fallot** causes **cyanosis**.
congenital-heart-shunts.intervention: **Defect closure** abolishes the shunt, while **prostaglandin** keeps the duct open when pulmonary or systemic flow depends on it before repair.
congenital-heart-shunts.adverse: Closure can cause **arrhythmia** or residual leak around a device, while **prostaglandin** can cause apnoea, fever and hypotension through vasodilation.

copd-emphysema-bronchitis.trigger: Prolonged inhalation of **cigarette smoke** and other irritants drives chronic airway inflammation and **oxidative stress** in susceptible lungs.
copd-emphysema-bronchitis.target: Small airways and alveolar walls are injured, involving **macrophages**, **neutrophils** and an imbalance between **proteases** and antiproteases.
copd-emphysema-bronchitis.mechanism: **Chronic bronchitis** produces excess mucus and airway narrowing, while **emphysema** destroys alveolar walls and reduces elastic recoil.
copd-emphysema-bronchitis.manifestation: Expiratory airflow limitation causes progressive **breathlessness**, chronic productive cough and **air trapping** with hyperinflation and **hypoxaemia**.
copd-emphysema-bronchitis.intervention: **Bronchodilators** relax airway smooth muscle, **inhaled corticosteroids** reduce exacerbation prone inflammation, and **smoking cessation** slows further lung destruction.
copd-emphysema-bronchitis.adverse: **Beta agonists** cause tremor and palpitations through systemic receptor stimulation, while **inhaled corticosteroids** predispose to oral candidiasis and pneumonia.

cough-mucus-drugs.trigger: Airway irritation, infection or thick retained mucus activates the **cough reflex** and makes **sputum clearance** difficult.
cough-mucus-drugs.target: The medullary **cough centre**, airway sensory nerves, mucus **disulphide bonds** and airway surface liquid control cough drive and sputum thickness.
cough-mucus-drugs.mechanism: Irritation triggers afferent signals to the **cough centre**, while dehydrated mucus with intact **disulphide bonds** stays thick, sticky and hard to clear by ciliary action.
cough-mucus-drugs.manifestation: This explains persistent **cough**, **sticky sputum**, wheeze from retained secretions and disturbed sleep, especially when mucus is thick and airway irritation continues.
cough-mucus-drugs.intervention: **Codeine** and **dextromethorphan** suppress the cough centre, **guaifenesin** increases airway fluid, and **acetylcysteine** and carbocisteine loosen mucus structure.
cough-mucus-drugs.adverse: Central suppressants cause **sedation**, constipation and respiratory depression with opioids, dextromethorphan causes dizziness, and mucolytics cause **nausea**, bronchospasm in susceptible patients and loose stools.

covid-19-pathogenesis.trigger: Inhaled **SARS-CoV-2** reaches airway epithelium where susceptible **type 2 pneumocytes** and nasal **epithelial cells** permit entry.
covid-19-pathogenesis.target: Viral **spike protein** binds the **ACE2 receptor** with **TMPRSS2 priming** on alveolar and **endothelial cells**.
covid-19-pathogenesis.mechanism: After entry the virus replicates in **host cells** and triggers **innate immunity** with release of **cytokines** that injure the **alveolar membrane**.
covid-19-pathogenesis.manifestation: **Diffuse alveolar damage** causes breathlessness with **hypoxia** while **endothelitis** with **microthrombi** worsens mismatch and prolongs fever and cough.
covid-19-pathogenesis.intervention: Early **antiviral** limits replication while **dexamethasone** dampens harmful **inflammation** in hypoxic disease, and **oxygen** corrects low saturation.
covid-19-pathogenesis.adverse: **dexamethasone** raises **blood glucose** and suppresses **immunity**, which invites secondary **infection**. Prolonged use retains fluid and slows wound healing.

cranial-nerve-lesions.trigger: Daily demands for vision, chewing, facial movement, hearing, swallowing and speech activate distinct **brainstem nuclei** and their **cranial nerves**.
cranial-nerve-lesions.target: Targets are nuclei in **midbrain**, **pons** and **medulla** plus their nerves, ganglia and target **muscles**.
cranial-nerve-lesions.mechanism: Each nucleus drives its nerve so a focal lesion silences one pathway while neighbouring **long tracts** may add weakness or **sensory loss**.
cranial-nerve-lesions.manifestation: Trigeminal lesions numb the **face** while facial lesions weaken expression, vagal lesions impair **swallowing** and hypoglossal lesions deviate the **tongue**. Eye mover lesions cause double vision with a drooping **eyelid**.
cranial-nerve-lesions.intervention: Care targets the **cause** such as stroke or tumour while **eye protection** with patching and **lubricants** shields the exposed cornea.
cranial-nerve-lesions.adverse: **Steroid** action raises **blood glucose** and disturbs sleep while prolonged patching blurs **vision** and dries surrounding **skin**.

cystic-fibrosis.trigger: Inheritance of two faulty **CFTR gene** copies, commonly with **F508del**, removes normal chloride channel function from epithelial surfaces.
cystic-fibrosis.target: Defective **CFTR chloride channels** in airway, pancreatic and sweat gland **epithelial cells** fail to reach or open at the apical membrane.
cystic-fibrosis.mechanism: Low chloride secretion with excessive **sodium absorption** dehydrates **airway surface liquid**, thickening mucus and impairing **ciliary clearance** of bacteria.
cystic-fibrosis.manifestation: Thick mucus causes chronic cough, recurrent **Pseudomonas** infection and **bronchiectasis**, plus pancreatic insufficiency, malabsorption and salty sweat with high **sweat chloride**.
cystic-fibrosis.intervention: **CFTR modulators** improve channel folding and opening, while **airway clearance** and **antibiotics** mobilise mucus and suppress chronic infection.
cystic-fibrosis.adverse: Modulators can cause **liver enzyme elevation**, headache and **drug interactions**, while inhaled antibiotics may cause **bronchospasm** and cough.

cytochrome-p450-interactions.trigger: A **drug substrate**, certain other medicines or **grapefruit** constituents reach the **liver** and alter how quickly drugs are cleared or activated.
cytochrome-p450-interactions.target: **Hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes**, especially in **hepatocytes**, oxidise lipid soluble drugs and some **prodrugs** in the endoplasmic reticulum.
cytochrome-p450-interactions.mechanism: **Inducers** increase enzyme synthesis and speed clearance, whereas **inhibitors** block enzyme activity and slow clearance, and some **prodrugs** need oxidation to become active.
cytochrome-p450-interactions.manifestation: Faster clearance causes **loss of efficacy** and treatment failure, whereas slower clearance causes drug accumulation, exaggerated effects and **toxicity**.
cytochrome-p450-interactions.intervention: Stopping or replacing an **inducer** or **inhibitor**, or choosing a drug not handled by the affected **enzyme**, restores predictable exposure.
cytochrome-p450-interactions.adverse: An **inhibitor** such as a **macrolide** can raise levels of a co-prescribed drug to toxicity, while an **inducer** can cause contraceptive or transplant drug failure.

deep-vein-thrombosis.trigger: The **Virchow triad** of venous stasis, endothelial injury and **hypercoagulability** from immobility, surgery, cancer or pregnancy starts clot formation.
deep-vein-thrombosis.target: Platelets and the **coagulation cascade** act at **venous valve pockets**, where slow flow favours fibrin formation and red cell trapping.
deep-vein-thrombosis.mechanism: Thrombin converts fibrinogen to **fibrin**, stabilising a growing **venous thrombus** that propagates proximally and may detach as an embolus.
deep-vein-thrombosis.manifestation: Calf or leg pain, swelling and tenderness reflect **venous obstruction**, while embolisation to pulmonary arteries causes **pulmonary embolism** with breathlessness and pleuritic pain.
deep-vein-thrombosis.intervention: **Anticoagulants** such as heparin and direct oral agents inhibit **thrombin** or factor Xa, preventing clot growth while natural fibrinolysis clears it.
deep-vein-thrombosis.adverse: **Anticoagulants** increase bleeding risk, including gastrointestinal and intracranial haemorrhage, and **heparin** can rarely cause heparin induced thrombocytopenia with paradoxical thrombosis.

dementia-drugs.trigger: Loss of **cholinergic neurons** in Alzheimer disease lowers acetylcholine signalling, while excess **glutamate** activity adds excitotoxic injury to failing **memory networks**.
dementia-drugs.target: Drugs inhibit **acetylcholinesterase** to preserve acetylcholine, or block the **NMDA receptor** channel to limit excess glutamate excitation.
dementia-drugs.mechanism: Less acetylcholine weakens **cholinergic signalling** for attention and memory, while persistent NMDA activation allows excess **calcium entry** that disturbs neurons and worsens **excitotoxicity**.
dementia-drugs.manifestation: Failing cholinergic and glutamate balance explains progressive **memory loss**, impaired **cognition** and language, and declining daily function in dementia.
dementia-drugs.intervention: **Donepezil** and other **cholinesterase inhibitors** raise acetylcholine by blocking its breakdown, while **memantine** blocks the NMDA channel to reduce excess excitation.
dementia-drugs.adverse: More acetylcholine causes **nausea and diarrhoea** and can slow the heart causing **bradycardia**, while **memantine** can cause dizziness and confusion.

dengue-fever.trigger: An **Aedes mosquito** bite inoculates **dengue virus**, with severe disease more likely during a second infection with a different serotype.
dengue-fever.target: Virus infects **monocytes** and dendritic cells, and immune mediators increase **capillary permeability**, especially as fever settles in the critical phase.
dengue-fever.mechanism: Plasma leaks from capillaries while **platelets** fall from marrow suppression and consumption, causing **haemoconcentration**, effusions and intravascular volume loss.
dengue-fever.manifestation: High fever, severe myalgia, rash and bleeding tendency occur first, then **plasma leakage** can cause ascites, pleural effusion and **shock** in the critical phase.
dengue-fever.intervention: Careful **intravenous fluids** replace leaked plasma with close monitoring, **paracetamol** controls fever, and platelet support is reserved for significant bleeding.
dengue-fever.adverse: Excess fluids can cause **fluid overload** and pulmonary oedema as leakage stops, and **NSAIDs** can worsen bleeding by impairing platelet function.

dependence-drugs.trigger: Repeated nicotine or alcohol use adapts **reward circuits**, so withdrawal and conditioned cues produce **craving** and relapse.
dependence-drugs.target: **Alpha4 beta2 nicotinic receptors**, **opioid receptors**, glutamate and GABA balance and **aldehyde dehydrogenase** control reward, craving and alcohol breakdown.
dependence-drugs.mechanism: Nicotine activates nicotinic receptors to release **dopamine** in reward pathways, alcohol enhances inhibition and alters glutamate balance, and **acetaldehyde** accumulates when its breakdown is blocked.
dependence-drugs.manifestation: Adaptation explains **withdrawal symptoms**, strong **craving**, loss of control and relapse after abstinence, with flushing and vomiting if acetaldehyde accumulates after drinking.
dependence-drugs.intervention: **Nicotine replacement** eases withdrawal, **varenicline** partly activates and blocks nicotinic receptors, **naltrexone** blocks opioid reward, **acamprosate** stabilises glutamate balance, and disulfiram blocks acetaldehyde breakdown.
dependence-drugs.adverse: Nicotine causes **nausea** and local irritation, varenicline causes nausea and vivid dreams, naltrexone causes nausea and blocks opioid analgesia, and **disulfiram** causes a severe flushing reaction with alcohol.

diabetic-complications.trigger: Chronic **hyperglycaemia** from insulin deficiency or **insulin resistance** exposes small and large vessels to years of metabolic injury.
diabetic-complications.target: Excess glucose injures **endothelial cells**, pericytes and neurons through **advanced glycation end products**, the polyol pathway, oxidative stress and protein kinase C.
diabetic-complications.mechanism: **Basement membrane** thickening, capillary leak and **atherosclerosis** narrow or occlude vessels, causing ischaemia and tissue damage in retina, kidney, nerve and arteries.
diabetic-complications.manifestation: **Retinopathy**, nephropathy with albuminuria, painful or numb **peripheral neuropathy**, myocardial infarction, stroke and limb ischaemia reflect the affected vascular bed.
diabetic-complications.intervention: Glucose control limits glycation injury, **blood pressure control** protects kidney and retina, and **statins** lower **LDL cholesterol** and plaque risk.
diabetic-complications.adverse: Intensive glucose lowering can cause **hypoglycaemia**, **ACE inhibitors** can cause cough and kidney dysfunction, and statins can cause muscle pain.

diarrhoea-ors.trigger: Toxins, unabsorbed solutes or invasive organisms disturb **intestinal fluid** handling. **Vibrio cholerae toxin** drives pure secretion, while mucosal invasion causes blood and mucus in stool.
diarrhoea-ors.target: The process acts on **enterocytes** lining the small and large bowel. The preserved rescue pathway is the **sodium glucose cotransporter** used by oral rehydration solution.
diarrhoea-ors.mechanism: Secretory diarrhoea pumps **chloride** and water into the lumen, osmotic diarrhoea retains solute and water, and invasive disease leaks blood and exudate. The **SGLT cotransporter** still absorbs sodium with glucose and water follows.
diarrhoea-ors.manifestation: Fluid loss causes **thirst**, dry mucosa, reduced urine and **sunken eyes**, progressing to weak pulse and shock. Children deteriorate fastest because reserves are small and losses continue.
diarrhoea-ors.intervention: **Oral rehydration solution** uses glucose linked sodium absorption to replace water and salts, while **intravenous fluids** rescue shock. **Antibiotics** help only selected invasive or cholera cases, and zinc aids recovery in children.
diarrhoea-ors.adverse: **Oral rehydration solution** fails when vomiting or shock prevents gut absorption and needs intravenous rescue. Unneeded **antibiotics** cause resistance, allergy and disturbance of normal gut flora.

digoxin-toxicity.trigger: Symptomatic **heart failure** or fast **atrial fibrillation** prompts **digoxin** therapy, and poor clearance or low potassium allows toxicity to build.
digoxin-toxicity.target: Targets are the myocardial **sodium potassium pump** plus coupled **sodium calcium exchange** and vagal slowing at the **AV node**.
digoxin-toxicity.mechanism: Pump blockade raises intracellular **sodium**, reverses **calcium** extrusion and strengthens contraction while vagal effect slows **AV conduction** toward block.
digoxin-toxicity.manifestation: Nausea, blurred vision with **yellow halos**, confusion and **bradycardia** occur with **AV block** and dangerous ventricular **arrhythmia**.
digoxin-toxicity.intervention: Stop **digoxin**, correct **potassium** and give **digoxin specific Fab fragments** to bind free drug in severe toxicity.
digoxin-toxicity.adverse: **Fab treatment** can cause falling **potassium** with rapid shifts and worsening **heart failure** plus rare **allergic reaction** to antibody protein.

disseminated-intravascular-coagulation.trigger: **Sepsis**, major **trauma**, malignancy and obstetric emergency release abundant **tissue factor** into blood. Systemic inflammation then triggers widespread coagulation.
disseminated-intravascular-coagulation.target: The targets are the **clotting cascade**, circulating **platelets** and small vessel **endothelium**. Unchecked thrombin generation consumes factors and natural inhibitors.
disseminated-intravascular-coagulation.mechanism: Exposed **tissue factor** drives excess **thrombin** with fibrin formation inside small vessels. **Platelets** and **fibrinogen** are consumed faster than marrow and liver replace them.
disseminated-intravascular-coagulation.manifestation: Microthrombi cause organ **ischaemia** while factor depletion causes **bleeding** from wounds and lines. Raised **D-dimer** with falling platelets marks overt disease.
disseminated-intravascular-coagulation.intervention: **Treat the cause** with antibiotics, delivery or surgery to stop **tissue factor** release at source. **Fibrinogen** with platelet replacement restores clotting power during active bleeding.
disseminated-intravascular-coagulation.adverse: **Platelet** and plasma replacement can cause circulatory **overload** with breathlessness. Donor antibodies may injure **lung** capillaries and worsen **hypoxia**.

diuretics.trigger: Salt and water overload from **heart failure**, kidney disease or **hypertension** creates the need to increase urinary sodium loss.
diuretics.target: Each class blocks a segment specific transporter, from **NKCC2** in the loop to **NCC** distally and **ENaC** or the mineralocorticoid receptor in the collecting duct.
diuretics.mechanism: Blocking **sodium transporters** keeps sodium and water in the tubule, so less is reabsorbed to blood. **Loop agents** act earliest among the potent sites and remove the most fluid.
diuretics.manifestation: Effective diuresis relieves **breathlessness**, **oedema** and raised blood pressure. The segment blocked predicts potassium, calcium and acid base changes seen on monitoring.
diuretics.intervention: **Furosemide** blocks NKCC2, **thiazides** block NCC, and **amiloride** or **spironolactone** limit collecting duct sodium uptake. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors act mainly in the proximal tubule.
diuretics.adverse: **Loop diuretics** and **thiazides** waste potassium and magnesium and can cause volume depletion. Potassium sparing agents can cause **hyperkalaemia**, and spironolactone can cause gynaecomastia.

dka-pathophysiology.trigger: Absolute or relative **insulin deficiency** plus raised **counter regulatory hormones**, often triggered by infection or missed insulin, starts unrestrained fuel breakdown.
dka-pathophysiology.target: Lack of insulin at **adipose tissue**, **liver** and **muscle** switches metabolism from glucose use and storage to fat and protein breakdown.
dka-pathophysiology.mechanism: **Lipolysis** releases fatty acids that the liver converts to **ketone bodies**, while **gluconeogenesis** and poor glucose uptake raise blood glucose.
dka-pathophysiology.manifestation: **Hyperglycaemia** causes **osmotic diuresis** with dehydration and sodium and potassium loss, while ketone acid causes deep **Kussmaul breathing**, vomiting and drowsiness.
dka-pathophysiology.intervention: **Intravenous fluids** restore circulation, **insulin** stops ketone production and lowers glucose, and monitored **potassium replacement** prevents treatment related depletion.
dka-pathophysiology.adverse: **Insulin** drives **potassium** into cells and can unmask total body depletion as falling blood potassium, causing weakness and **cardiac arrhythmia** if not replaced.

dna-replication-repair.trigger: Cell division requires faithful **DNA replication**, while **ultraviolet light** and spontaneous replication errors continually damage the DNA template.
dna-replication-repair.target: Fork enzymes **helicase**, **primase**, **DNA polymerase** and **ligase** copy DNA, and separate repair pathways correct specific lesions.
dna-replication-repair.mechanism: Leading strand synthesis is continuous and the lagging strand uses **Okazaki fragments**; **excision repair**, mismatch repair and recombination fix damage.
dna-replication-repair.manifestation: Repair defects cause **xeroderma pigmentosum** with sun sensitivity and skin cancers, and **Lynch syndrome** with colorectal cancer from mismatch failure.
dna-replication-repair.intervention: **Sunscreen** and avoidance prevent ultraviolet dimers, while **PARP inhibitors** exploit defective recombination repair selectively in cancer cells.
dna-replication-repair.adverse: **PARP inhibitors** also affect normal dividing cells, causing **bone marrow suppression**, nausea and fatigue from impaired DNA repair.

dopaminergic-drugs.trigger: Imbalance of **dopamine** signalling starts the clinical problem, with deficiency causing parkinsonism and excess signalling in limbic pathways contributing to **psychosis**.
dopaminergic-drugs.target: The targets are **D1 receptors** coupled to stimulatory G proteins and **D2 receptors** coupled to inhibitory G proteins on striatal and limbic neurons.
dopaminergic-drugs.mechanism: **D1 receptor** activation raises **cyclic AMP** and promotes movement through the direct pathway, while **D2 receptor** activation lowers cyclic AMP and restrains the indirect pathway.
dopaminergic-drugs.manifestation: Low striatal **dopamine** causes **bradykinesia**, rigidity, and tremor, while excess mesolimbic **D2 signalling** contributes to hallucinations and delusions in psychosis.
dopaminergic-drugs.intervention: **Levodopa** raises dopamine supply, **dopamine agonists** stimulate receptors directly, **D2 blockers** treat psychosis, and **aripiprazole** type drugs act as partial agonists that stabilise signalling.
dopaminergic-drugs.adverse: **D2 blockers** cause **parkinsonism**, prolactin rise, and tardive dyskinesia from striatal and pituitary blockade, while **levodopa** and agonists cause dyskinesia, nausea, hallucinations, and impulse control problems.

dose-response-receptors.trigger: Exposure to a **drug** at increasing concentration triggers progressive **receptor occupancy** and a measurable response.
dose-response-receptors.target: Specific **receptors** and their downstream **signalling pathways** determine potency, maximal effect and tissue selectivity.
dose-response-receptors.mechanism: A **full agonist** produces maximal response, a **partial agonist** produces a submaximal ceiling, and antagonists reduce activation by occupancy or by lowering efficacy.
dose-response-receptors.manifestation: The **dose response curve** shows potency by position and efficacy by ceiling, explaining why increasing exposure eventually gives no further **therapeutic benefit**.
dose-response-receptors.intervention: A **competitive antagonist** shifts the curve right and is surmountable, while a **noncompetitive antagonist** lowers maximal response despite higher agonist concentration.
dose-response-receptors.adverse: A **partial agonist** can act as a functional antagonist in presence of a full agonist, reducing response and causing **loss of efficacy** or withdrawal effects.

dyslipidaemia-statin-pathway.trigger: Excess hepatic cholesterol production, dietary load or an inherited **LDL receptor** defect raises circulating **LDL cholesterol**.
dyslipidaemia-statin-pathway.target: Hepatic **HMG-CoA reductase** makes cholesterol, **LDL receptors** clear LDL from blood, and an intestinal cholesterol transporter absorbs dietary cholesterol.
dyslipidaemia-statin-pathway.mechanism: The liver packages cholesterol into **VLDL** that becomes **LDL**, peripheral tissues return cholesterol via **HDL**, and defective receptors impair LDL clearance.
dyslipidaemia-statin-pathway.manifestation: Sustained high LDL drives **atherosclerosis** causing premature coronary disease, while familial disease adds tendon **xanthomata** and early family events.
dyslipidaemia-statin-pathway.intervention: A **statin** blocks cholesterol synthesis and upregulates LDL receptors, **ezetimibe** blocks gut absorption, and **PCSK9 inhibition** preserves hepatic receptors.
dyslipidaemia-statin-pathway.adverse: **Statins** can cause muscle symptoms and raised liver enzymes, **ezetimibe** can cause gastrointestinal upset, and **PCSK9 inhibitors** mainly cause injection site reactions.

ectopic-pregnancy.trigger: Tubal injury from **pelvic infection**, smoking or **tubal surgery** delays transport so the **fertilised ovum** implants in the tube.
ectopic-pregnancy.target: The target is the **fallopian tube** wall, especially the **ampulla**, invaded by proliferating **trophoblast** tissue.
ectopic-pregnancy.mechanism: Invading **trophoblast** erodes tubal vessels and thin **tubal wall** so the pregnancy leaks or **ruptures** with blood into the abdomen.
ectopic-pregnancy.manifestation: **Pelvic pain** with vaginal bleeding and later **haemoperitoneum** explains fainting and **shock**, with slowly rising pregnancy hormone.
ectopic-pregnancy.intervention: **Methotrexate** halts dividing trophoblast in stable cases, while **surgery** removes the ectopic and **expectant care** suits small resolving cases.
ectopic-pregnancy.adverse: **Methotrexate** blocks folate use so it can cause mouth sores, **liver injury** and **bone marrow suppression**.

electron-transport-chain.trigger: Energy demand drives oxidation of **NADH** and **FADH2** produced by glycolysis and the **TCA cycle** in mitochondria.
electron-transport-chain.target: Inner mitochondrial **complexes I to IV**, **coenzyme Q**, cytochrome c and **ATP synthase** carry electrons and make ATP.
electron-transport-chain.mechanism: Electrons flow to **oxygen**, protons are pumped into the **intermembrane space**, and their return through **ATP synthase** drives ATP formation.
electron-transport-chain.manifestation: Chain failure reduces **ATP**, causing **lactic acidosis**, muscle weakness and encephalopathy, while uncoupling releases the stored energy as heat.
electron-transport-chain.intervention: Removing the **inhibitor** or uncoupler and giving supportive **oxygen** restores electron flow and **ATP synthase** activity where possible.
electron-transport-chain.adverse: An **antidote** that binds the inhibitor can also bind essential **metal ions**, and excess **oxygen** can increase reactive oxygen injury.

endocrine-feedback-axes.trigger: Failure or excess at the hypothalamus, pituitary or target gland disturbs **negative feedback** control of the **thyroid axis** and **adrenal axis**.
endocrine-feedback-axes.target: Each axis links the **hypothalamus**, **anterior pituitary** and a target gland such as the thyroid or adrenal cortex through releasing and trophic hormones.
endocrine-feedback-axes.mechanism: Falling end hormone reduces feedback and raises **trophic hormone** output in **primary failure**, while pituitary or hypothalamic failure gives low trophic drive despite low end hormone. Excess reverses this pattern.
endocrine-feedback-axes.manifestation: **Primary gland failure** shows low end hormone with high trophic hormone, while **secondary failure** shows low end hormone with low or inappropriately normal trophic hormone. Pituitary excess raises both levels.
endocrine-feedback-axes.intervention: **Hormone replacement** restores a missing end hormone, **suppressive therapy** or blockade reduces excess hormone action, and **surgery** removes an overactive gland or pituitary source.
endocrine-feedback-axes.adverse: Excess **replacement hormone** causes symptoms of hormone excess by overactivating target receptors, while excessive **suppression** can push the axis into deficiency with fatigue and metabolic slowing.

endometriosis.trigger: **Retrograde menstruation** seeds viable **endometrial cells** into the pelvis where they implant outside the uterus.
endometriosis.target: Targets are **peritoneum**, **ovaries** and ectopic **endometrial implants** that respond to cyclic ovarian hormones.
endometriosis.mechanism: Ectopic tissue bleeds each cycle, driving **inflammation**, fibrosis, **adhesions** and blood filled **chocolate cysts**.
endometriosis.manifestation: **Dysmenorrhoea**, deep **dyspareunia** and chronic pelvic pain occur with **subfertility** from distorted anatomy and inflammation.
endometriosis.intervention: **Hormonal suppression** stops cycling and shrinks implants while **surgery** excises implants and drains **endometriomas** to restore anatomy.
endometriosis.adverse: **GnRH analogue** action causes **hot flushes** and bone loss while surgery risks **adhesions** and reduced ovarian reserve.

enzyme-kinetics-inhibition.trigger: Rising **substrate load** during feeding or signalling creates demand for faster action. Need for tight control makes excess **enzyme activity** the problem to tune.
enzyme-kinetics-inhibition.target: The **enzyme active site** for substrate binding, a distant **allosteric site** for modulators, and measured **reaction rate** are the targets.
enzyme-kinetics-inhibition.mechanism: **Competitive inhibition** raises apparent **Km** without changing maximum rate at the active site. **Non competitive inhibition** lowers **maximum rate** without changing Km from elsewhere.
enzyme-kinetics-inhibition.manifestation: Competitive block is overcome by more **substrate concentration** on **Michaelis Menten** plots. Non competitive block stays low and shows altered **Lineweaver Burk** intercepts.
enzyme-kinetics-inhibition.intervention: Extra **substrate supply** overcomes competitive block by outcompeting inhibitor. Removing drug or adding **allosteric modulator** tuning eases non competitive block.
enzyme-kinetics-inhibition.adverse: Excess inhibitor causes **pathway shutdown** with upstream **substrate build up** and toxicity. Off target **enzyme blockade** adds nausea and rash from related pathways.

epilepsy-seizure.trigger: A hyperexcitable focus arises from **channelopathy**, cortical injury or metabolic disturbance. Loss of inhibitory control lets excitation outrun inhibition in **cortical neurons**.
epilepsy-seizure.target: The balance depends on **voltage gated sodium channels**, **GABA receptors** and **glutamate receptors**. Excess glutamate drive or reduced GABA inhibition lowers the seizure threshold.
epilepsy-seizure.mechanism: Neurons fire in hypersynchronous bursts as **sodium influx** sustains depolarisation and **glutamate** excites neighbours. When recruitment spreads beyond the focus, focal activity becomes generalised across both hemispheres.
epilepsy-seizure.manifestation: A **focal seizure** causes localised jerking, sensory change or impaired awareness depending on cortex involved. A **generalised tonic clonic seizure** causes whole body convulsions, tongue biting and postictal confusion.
epilepsy-seizure.intervention: **Sodium channel blockers** reduce repetitive firing, **GABA enhancers** strengthen inhibition and **glutamate blockers** reduce excitation. Choice depends on seizure type and spread shown in the figure.
epilepsy-seizure.adverse: **Sodium channel blockers** can cause dizziness and hyponatraemia from their membrane stabilising action. **GABA enhancers** cause sedation and dependence because enhanced inhibition depresses alertness and coordination.

extradural-subdural-haematoma.trigger: Head **trauma** tears the **middle meningeal artery** or bridging **veins**, spilling blood between skull, dura and brain.
extradural-subdural-haematoma.target: Targets are the **extradural space**, **subdural space** and underlying **brain tissue** compressed by the collection.
extradural-subdural-haematoma.mechanism: Arterial bleeding strips dura into a **lens shaped** clot while torn **bridging veins** spread a **crescent shaped** sheet that shifts brain.
extradural-subdural-haematoma.manifestation: A lucid interval then rapid **coma** marks extradural bleed while fluctuating **consciousness**, weakness and **herniation** signs mark subdural pressure.
extradural-subdural-haematoma.intervention: **Surgical evacuation** through burr holes or **craniotomy** removes clot while **intracranial pressure** care with head elevation buys time.
extradural-subdural-haematoma.adverse: **Surgery** risks bleeding, wound **infection** and **seizures** while pressure measures cause fluid shifts and **electrolyte** disturbance.

fetal-circulation-birth-transition.trigger: Birth with **cord clamping** and the **first breath** replaces placental flow with lung oxygenation and raises systemic demand.
fetal-circulation-birth-transition.target: The targets are the **ductus venosus**, **foramen ovale** and **ductus arteriosus** linking umbilical, liver and lung circuits.
fetal-circulation-birth-transition.mechanism: Lung expansion lowers **pulmonary resistance** while rising **oxygen** and falling **prostaglandin** constrict and close the shunts.
fetal-circulation-birth-transition.manifestation: Successful closure separates **oxygen rich** and **oxygen poor** streams while persistent shunts cause **murmur** and duct dependent cyanosis.
fetal-circulation-birth-transition.intervention: **Prostaglandin** infusion keeps the **ductus arteriosus** open to preserve flow in duct dependent lesions before surgery.
fetal-circulation-birth-transition.adverse: **Indomethacin** closes the duct by blocking **prostaglandin** synthesis but risks **renal impairment** and gut injury from the same action.

fibrinolytics-antifibrinolytics.trigger: Vessel injury and **thrombosis** build a fibrin clot that may need breakdown, while active bleeding needs clot protection from **plasmin**.
fibrinolytics-antifibrinolytics.target: **Plasminogen** conversion to plasmin, **fibrin** in the clot, and plasminogen binding sites blocked by tranexamic acid are the central targets.
fibrinolytics-antifibrinolytics.mechanism: **Plasmin** digests **fibrin** and dissolves clot, fibrinolytics accelerate plasmin formation from plasminogen, and tranexamic acid blocks plasminogen binding to fibrin so plasmin cannot act.
fibrinolytics-antifibrinolytics.manifestation: Occlusive clot explains **myocardial infarction** and ischaemic stroke symptoms, while excessive fibrinolysis explains persistent **bleeding** after trauma, surgery or childbirth.
fibrinolytics-antifibrinolytics.intervention: **Alteplase** and streptokinase generate plasmin to lyse occlusive clot, while **tranexamic acid** preserves clot and reduces bleeding in haemorrhage.
fibrinolytics-antifibrinolytics.adverse: Fibrinolytics cause **bleeding**, including intracranial haemorrhage and allergy with streptokinase, while tranexamic acid can cause nausea and, rarely, **thrombosis** or seizures at high exposure.

fluid-balance-hormones.trigger: Raised **plasma osmolality**, volume depletion or hormone deficiency threatens water, salt and pressure balance, while excess vasopressin action retains too much **water**.
fluid-balance-hormones.target: Vasopressin acts on **V2 receptors** in the collecting duct and **V1 receptors** on vessels, while aldosterone like drugs act on **mineralocorticoid receptors**.
fluid-balance-hormones.mechanism: V2 activation inserts **aquaporin channels** to reclaim water, mineralocorticoid activation increases **sodium reabsorption** with water following, and V1 activation causes **vasoconstriction**.
fluid-balance-hormones.manifestation: Deficiency explains **polyuria** and dehydration in diabetes insipidus, salt wasting with **hypotension** in adrenal failure, and dilutional **hyponatraemia** when water is retained.
fluid-balance-hormones.intervention: **Desmopressin** stimulates V2 receptors, **vasopressin** stimulates V1 and V2 receptors, **fludrocortisone** replaces mineralocorticoid action, and **tolvaptan** blocks V2 receptors.
fluid-balance-hormones.adverse: Excess V2 action causes **water retention** and hyponatraemia, fludrocortisone causes **hypertension** and potassium loss, and V2 blockade causes marked **polyuria** and thirst.

fluid-electrolytes-na-k.trigger: Changes in water intake or loss, salt balance, kidney handling or shifts between fluid compartments disturb **sodium concentration** and **potassium balance**.
fluid-electrolytes-na-k.target: **Antidiuretic hormone** and the **kidney** regulate water and sodium, while most potassium sits inside cells and small extracellular changes affect excitable tissues.
fluid-electrolytes-na-k.mechanism: Water excess dilutes sodium and water deficit concentrates it, moving water across **cell membranes** by **osmosis**. Potassium shifts and kidney losses or retention change the **resting membrane potential**.
fluid-electrolytes-na-k.manifestation: Sodium disorders mainly affect the **brain**, causing confusion, seizures or coma from swelling or shrinkage, while potassium disorders alter the **ECG** and cause weakness or arrhythmia.
fluid-electrolytes-na-k.intervention: **Water restriction** treats dilutional low sodium, **saline** replaces water and salt deficit, and **potassium replacement** treats depletion while shifting or removing potassium treats excess.
fluid-electrolytes-na-k.adverse: Too rapid **saline** correction of chronic low sodium can cause **osmotic demyelination**, while excess **potassium replacement** can cause dangerous hyperkalaemia and **cardiac arrhythmia**.

fracture-healing.trigger: A **fracture** tears bone and vessels, so bleeding forms a **haematoma** that fills the gap. The clot provides a scaffold and signals that start repair.
fracture-healing.target: The targets are **periosteal progenitor cells**, **chondroblasts** and **osteoblasts** at the fracture ends. **Osteoclasts** later reshape the new bone.
fracture-healing.mechanism: Inflammation clears debris, then **fibrocartilage** forms a soft callus bridging the gap. **Osteoblasts** mineralise this into woven bone as a hard callus, which **osteoclasts** remodel into lamellar bone.
fracture-healing.manifestation: Early swelling and pain reflect the **haematoma** and **inflammation**. Loss of stability and deformity reflect the gap, while poor blood supply or movement causes **delayed union** or **nonunion**.
fracture-healing.intervention: **Immobilisation** with a cast or splint and **internal fixation** with plates or nails hold alignment and reduce strain. This allows the **callus** to bridge and mineralise without disruption.
fracture-healing.adverse: Prolonged **immobilisation** causes joint stiffness and **muscle wasting** from disuse. **Internal fixation** carries risks of infection and hardware irritation because surgery breaches skin and periosteal blood supply.

fungal-infections.trigger: Warm moist skin, mucosal injury or **immune suppression** lets **dermatophytes**, **Candida** or inhaled spores establish infection.
fungal-infections.target: Targets are skin **keratin**, mucosal surfaces and lung tissue plus fungal **ergosterol** membranes and **glucan** walls.
fungal-infections.mechanism: **Ergosterol** keeps fungal membranes intact and **glucan** strengthens walls, allowing surface growth or deep **tissue invasion** when immunity fails.
fungal-infections.manifestation: Surface fungi cause scaly **tinea** and nail change, **Candida** causes thrush, and invasive disease causes lung lesions and **meningitis**.
fungal-infections.intervention: **Topical azoles** treat skin disease, systemic **azoles** block ergosterol synthesis, and **echinocandins** or polyenes treat invasive infection.
fungal-infections.adverse: **Azoles** can injure the **liver** and alter other drug levels, while **amphotericin** can damage kidneys and disturb salts through membrane action.

gaba-sedatives.trigger: Anxiety, insomnia, seizures, or anaesthesia induction creates a need to reduce **neuronal excitability**. Excess excitation can present as agitation, **seizures**, or inability to tolerate procedures.
gaba-sedatives.target: The **GABA-A receptor** chloride channel is the target, with separate binding sites for **benzodiazepines** and **barbiturates**. GABA itself opens the channel.
gaba-sedatives.mechanism: Benzodiazepines increase how often GABA opens the **chloride channel**, while barbiturates increase how long it stays open. Chloride entry hyperpolarises the **neuron** and reduces firing.
gaba-sedatives.manifestation: Enhanced inhibition produces calm, sleep, **anxiolysis**, and seizure control. Excess effect causes sedation, impaired memory, ataxia, and **respiratory depression**.
gaba-sedatives.intervention: **Benzodiazepines** treat anxiety, seizures, and procedural sedation, while **barbiturates** are reserved for selected anaesthesia or refractory seizures. **Flumazenil** antagonises the benzodiazepine site.
gaba-sedatives.adverse: Sedatives cause dependence, tolerance, falls, and **respiratory depression**, especially with alcohol or opioids. **Barbiturates** have a narrow safety margin and can cause coma and cardiovascular depression.

gallstone-formation-cholecystitis.trigger: **Cholesterol supersaturation** of bile with **gallbladder stasis** starts stone formation. Excess **hepatic cholesterol** secretion plus poor emptying favours nucleation.
gallstone-formation-cholecystitis.target: **Gallbladder bile** with dissolved **cholesterol crystals** and **pigment salts** is the target. Sluggish **gallbladder motility** lets sludge settle and grow.
gallstone-formation-cholecystitis.mechanism: **Cholesterol crystals** nucleate with mucin into sludge and hard **cholesterol stones**. Red cell breakdown forms black **pigment stones** while infection favours brown **pigment stones**.
gallstone-formation-cholecystitis.manifestation: Passing stones cause cramping **biliary colic** with vomiting after fatty meals. Impacted stone gives **cholecystitis** with fever, while **common bile duct** blockage causes **obstructive jaundice**.
gallstone-formation-cholecystitis.intervention: **Cholecystectomy** removes the stone forming gallbladder and prevents repeat attacks. Trapped duct stones are cleared by **ERCP**, while **analgesia** relieves pain only.
gallstone-formation-cholecystitis.adverse: **Cholecystectomy** can injure the **bile duct** or leave loose stools from continuous bile flow. **ERCP** can trigger **pancreatitis** with pain or bleeding from the cut papilla.

gastric-acid.trigger: A **meal** starts the process, as food and **gastric distension** trigger neural and hormonal signals that prepare the stomach for digestion.
gastric-acid.target: The target cell is the **parietal cell**, bearing **H2 receptors** and **M3 receptors** that converge with gastrin signalling on the **proton pump**.
gastric-acid.mechanism: **Histamine**, **gastrin**, and **acetylcholine** each stimulate the parietal cell, and their combined signal activates the **H+/K+ ATPase** to secrete hydrogen ions into the lumen.
gastric-acid.manifestation: Excess **gastric acid** injures the **oesophageal** and **duodenal mucosa**, producing heartburn, epigastric pain, ulceration, and bleeding when mucosal defence is overwhelmed.
gastric-acid.intervention: **H2 blockers** block the histamine signal, **proton pump inhibitors** such as omeprazole type drugs irreversibly block the **H+/K+ ATPase**, and **antimuscarinics** reduce vagal drive.
gastric-acid.adverse: **Proton pump inhibitors** reduce absorption of **magnesium** and vitamin B12 with prolonged use, while cimetidine type **H2 blockers** inhibit drug metabolising enzymes and raise other drug levels.

general-anaesthetics.trigger: Surgical stimulation requires reversible loss of **consciousness**, **memory** and **pain perception**, so anaesthetic drugs must quieten brain arousal systems.
general-anaesthetics.target: **GABA-A receptors**, **NMDA receptors** and several **ion channels** in cortical and subcortical neurons control inhibition, excitation and arousal.
general-anaesthetics.mechanism: Enhancing **GABA inhibition** or blocking **glutamate excitation** reduces neuronal firing, while volatile agents act at multiple channels to produce wide quieting of **brain networks**.
general-anaesthetics.manifestation: Balanced quieting produces **unconsciousness**, **amnesia**, analgesia and immobility, with dose dependent depression of breathing and **cardiovascular function**.
general-anaesthetics.intervention: **Propofol** and **thiopentone** enhance GABA-A action, **ketamine** blocks NMDA receptors, and **sevoflurane** and other volatile agents depress multiple channels.
general-anaesthetics.adverse: Propofol causes **hypotension** and **respiratory depression**, ketamine raises heart rate and can cause emergence phenomena, and volatile agents can trigger **malignant hyperthermia** in susceptible patients.

gerd-barrett-oesophagus.trigger: Weak **lower oesophageal sphincter** tone with **hiatus hernia** and raised **gastric pressure** lets acid reflux upward after meals.
gerd-barrett-oesophagus.target: The target is the **lower oesophageal sphincter**, **squamous mucosa** and distal **oesophageal epithelium** exposed to acid and pepsin.
gerd-barrett-oesophagus.mechanism: Repeated **acid exposure** injures **squamous cells** and drives inflammation, then intestinal **metaplasia** replaces damaged lining in Barrett change.
gerd-barrett-oesophagus.manifestation: Injury explains **heartburn**, painful swallowing and **oesophagitis**, while persistent **Barrett metaplasia** carries later cancer risk.
gerd-barrett-oesophagus.intervention: **Lifestyle measures** reduce reflux, **proton pump inhibitors** suppress acid to heal mucosa, and ablation or **fundoplication** treats Barrett or hernia.
gerd-barrett-oesophagus.adverse: **Proton pump inhibitors** can cause headache and **gut infection** risk from low acid, while **fundoplication** can cause swallowing difficulty and bloating.

gestational-diabetes.trigger: Placental hormones including human placental **lactogen** create maternal **insulin resistance** by mid gestation. Limited **beta cell** compensation lets glucose rise.
gestational-diabetes.target: Targets are maternal **insulin receptors**, pancreatic **beta cells** and placental transfer to the **fetus**. Resistance spares glucose for fetal growth.
gestational-diabetes.mechanism: Rising **progesterone** with cortisol impairs **insulin receptor** signalling while beta cells lag behind demand. Excess maternal **glucose** crosses the placenta and drives fetal **insulin** release.
gestational-diabetes.manifestation: Mothers often feel well but face **polyhydramnios** with higher **caesarean** likelihood when babies grow large. Fetal overgrowth causes **macrosomia** with neonatal **hypoglycaemia** after delivery.
gestational-diabetes.intervention: **Diet and exercise** lower after meal glucose and improve **insulin** sensitivity without drugs. **Insulin** therapy safely controls refractory **hyperglycaemia** in pregnancy.
gestational-diabetes.adverse: **Insulin** may cause maternal **hypoglycaemia** with shakiness from excess uptake. **Metformin** may cause nausea with gut cramps through intestinal effects.

gi-bleeding-upper-lower.trigger: Ruptured **peptic ulcer**, swollen **oesophageal varices** or bleeding **diverticula** start luminal blood loss. Mucosal erosion or vessel rupture opens the leak.
gi-bleeding-upper-lower.target: Upper **gut mucosa** above the duodenum, lower **colonic mucosa** below it, and circulating **blood volume** are the targets.
gi-bleeding-upper-lower.mechanism: Breached **mucosal vessels** spill **whole blood** into the gut lumen. Falling **blood volume** plus lower **haemoglobin level** reduce perfusion and oxygen carriage.
gi-bleeding-upper-lower.manifestation: Upper loss shows as **haematemesis** or black melaena, while lower loss shows as **haematochezia**. Growing loss brings tachycardia, hypotension and **shock** with collapse.
gi-bleeding-upper-lower.intervention: **Fluid resuscitation** plus blood transfusion restores volume and oxygen carriage. Urgent **endoscopic therapy** clips the source, with **embolisation** when endoscopy fails.
gi-bleeding-upper-lower.adverse: Large **blood transfusion** risks **volume overload** with breathlessness from raised filling pressures. Endoscopy during active vomiting risks **aspiration pneumonia** into lungs.

gi-hormones-secretion.trigger: Sight and smell of food, gastric distension and arrival of chyme in the **duodenum** trigger phased **gastrointestinal hormone** release.
gi-hormones-secretion.target: **Gastrin**, **cholecystokinin**, **secretin** and **somatostatin** act on stomach, pancreas, gallbladder and acid secreting cells.
gi-hormones-secretion.mechanism: Gastrin stimulates **parietal cells** to secrete acid, secretin promotes **bicarbonate secretion**, and cholecystokinin drives enzyme release and **gallbladder contraction**.
gi-hormones-secretion.manifestation: Coordinated secretion enables **digestion** and protects duodenal mucosa, while excess acid activity contributes to **dyspepsia** and **peptic ulceration**.
gi-hormones-secretion.intervention: A **proton pump inhibitor** blocks the final acid pump in parietal cells, while a **somatostatin analogue** suppresses multiple gastrointestinal hormones and secretions.
gi-hormones-secretion.adverse: Long term **proton pump inhibitor** use reduces acid defence and nutrient absorption, increasing risk of **enteric infection** and **magnesium wasting**.

gi-motility-drugs.trigger: Constipation, diarrhoea or disordered **enteric nerve** activity alters propulsion, secretion and **luminal water**, changing stool frequency and consistency.
gi-motility-drugs.target: **Enteric nerves** and gut smooth muscle control propulsion, mucosal transport controls **luminal water**, and **opioid receptors** and enkephalin breakdown control motility and secretion.
gi-motility-drugs.mechanism: Stimulants increase **enteric nerve** activity and propulsion, osmotics retain **water** in the lumen, opioids slow transit, and **racecadotril** preserves enkephalins to reduce secretion.
gi-motility-drugs.manifestation: Increased propulsion and water give **loose frequent stools**, while slowed transit gives **constipation**, abdominal discomfort and harder stools from greater water absorption.
gi-motility-drugs.intervention: **Senna** stimulates propulsion, **macrogol** and lactulose act osmotically, **loperamide** slows transit through opioid receptors, and racecadotril reduces intestinal secretion.
gi-motility-drugs.adverse: Stimulants cause **abdominal cramps**, osmotics cause bloating and diarrhoea if excessive, **loperamide** can cause constipation and ileus, and antisecretory drugs mainly cause headache and nausea.

gi-protectants-bile.trigger: Exposure of injured mucosa to **acid and pepsin**, or accumulation of **toxic bile acids** in **cholestasis**, drives ongoing gut and liver injury.
gi-protectants-bile.target: Sucralfate and bismuth act at the **ulcer surface**, while ursodeoxycholic acid acts on the **bile acid pool** and **hepatocyte** membranes.
gi-protectants-bile.mechanism: Sucralfate forms a protective **ulcer barrier**, bismuth coats ulcers and supports **prostaglandin** defence, and ursodeoxycholic acid replaces toxic bile acids and stabilises **cell membranes**.
gi-protectants-bile.manifestation: Less acid attack allows **mucosal healing** and pain relief, while less toxic bile acid injury reduces **pruritus** and protects liver and bile duct cells.
gi-protectants-bile.intervention: **Sucralfate** and **bismuth** protect damaged lining, while **ursodeoxycholic acid** treats cholestatic liver disease by making bile less injurious.
gi-protectants-bile.adverse: Sucralfate can cause **constipation** and bind other drugs, bismuth can darken the **stool** and tongue, and ursodeoxycholic acid commonly causes **diarrhoea**.

glaucoma-aqueous.trigger: Impaired aqueous outflow from ageing, a thickened **trabecular meshwork** or a crowded anterior segment starts pressure rise. Acute closure follows **pupillary block** in a shallow chamber.
glaucoma-aqueous.target: Aqueous is made by the **ciliary body** and drains through the **trabecular meshwork** and uveoscleral route. Resistance at outflow raises **intraocular pressure** that injures the optic nerve.
glaucoma-aqueous.mechanism: Raised **intraocular pressure** compresses axons at the **optic disc**, causing cupping and ganglion cell death. In closed angle, iris bows forward and blocks the **trabecular meshwork** abruptly.
glaucoma-aqueous.manifestation: Chronic open angle disease causes painless peripheral **visual field loss** with optic **cupping**. Acute closed angle causes severe eye pain, haloes, a mid dilated pupil and nausea.
glaucoma-aqueous.intervention: Aqueous suppressant drops such as **beta blockers** reduce production at the ciliary body, while **prostaglandin analogues** increase uveoscleral outflow. **Laser peripheral iridotomy** bypasses pupillary block in closed angle.
glaucoma-aqueous.adverse: **Beta blocker drops** can cause bronchospasm and bradycardia from systemic beta blockade. **Prostaglandin analogues** cause iris darkening and eyelash growth from local prostaglandin effects on melanocytes.

glaucoma-drugs.trigger: Raised **intraocular pressure** from excess aqueous production or poor drainage damages the **optic nerve** in glaucoma.
glaucoma-drugs.target: Drugs act on the **ciliary body** to reduce aqueous formation or on **trabecular** and **uveoscleral** pathways to increase drainage.
glaucoma-drugs.mechanism: Beta blockers and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors reduce **aqueous production**, alpha agonists reduce production and aid outflow, prostaglandins increase **uveoscleral outflow**, and miotics open **trabecular outflow**.
glaucoma-drugs.manifestation: Lower eye pressure slows **visual field loss** and optic nerve damage, even though most patients have no pain or early **symptoms**.
glaucoma-drugs.intervention: **Latanoprost** increases uveoscleral drainage, **timolol** reduces aqueous production, **brimonidine** does both partly, and **pilocarpine** increases trabecular drainage.
glaucoma-drugs.adverse: Timolol can cause **bronchospasm** and bradycardia, latanoprost causes **iris darkening** and longer lashes, and pilocarpine causes **miosis** with dim vision.

glomerulonephritis.trigger: **Infection**, **IgA dysregulation** or **autoantibody formation** initiates immune attack on the glomerular filter.
glomerulonephritis.target: **Glomerular basement membrane**, **podocytes** and **mesangial cells** are injured through immune deposits.
glomerulonephritis.mechanism: **Immune complexes** activate **complement** and attract **neutrophils**, causing proliferation, crescents and filter leaks.
glomerulonephritis.manifestation: **Haematuria** and **proteinuria** with **hypertension** and swelling reflect nephritic inflammation and falling filtration.
glomerulonephritis.intervention: **Corticosteroids** with **immunosuppression** calm immune injury, alongside **supportive care** controlling pressure and swelling.
glomerulonephritis.adverse: **Corticosteroids** plus **immunosuppression** increase **infection risk** through broad dampening of protective immunity.

glucocorticoid-effects.trigger: Severe **inflammation**, allergy, autoimmune disease or adrenal failure creates the need for potent **glucocorticoid** action or replacement.
