menstrual-cycle-axis.manifestation: **Ovulation** pain and fertile mucus mark midcycle while failed or disordered cycling causes **amenorrhoea** or irregular **bleeding**.
menstrual-cycle-axis.intervention: The **combined pill** blocks ovulation with estrogen plus progestogen while **progestogen only** methods thicken **cervical mucus** and thin endometrium.
menstrual-cycle-axis.adverse: **Estrogen** action risks **venous thrombosis** and nausea while progestogen action causes breakthrough **bleeding** and breast tenderness.

metabolic-acidosis-anion-gap.trigger: Either added **acid** from ketoacidosis, lactate or toxins, or lost **bicarbonate** from gut or kidney, lowers blood **pH**.
metabolic-acidosis-anion-gap.target: The **bicarbonate buffer** in blood is consumed first, while the **lungs** and **kidneys** attempt compensation and acid excretion.
metabolic-acidosis-anion-gap.mechanism: Added unmeasured **anions** widen the **anion gap**, whereas bicarbonate loss is balanced by rising **chloride**, keeping the gap normal.
metabolic-acidosis-anion-gap.manifestation: Acidaemia causes deep rapid **Kussmaul breathing**, impaired cardiac contractility and confusion, while the gap pattern points to the underlying **cause**.
metabolic-acidosis-anion-gap.intervention: Treating the **underlying cause** is primary, **dialysis** clears dialysable acids and toxins, and given **bicarbonate** is reserved for selected severe cases.
metabolic-acidosis-anion-gap.adverse: Given **bicarbonate** can worsen intracellular acidosis through generated **carbon dioxide**, and can cause hypernatraemia, hypokalaemia and volume **overload**.

migraine-drugs.trigger: Activation of the **trigeminovascular system** during a migraine attack releases **CGRP** and other mediators that amplify pain signalling.
migraine-drugs.target: **CGRP receptors** and CGRP itself, **5-HT1B/1D receptors** on vessels and trigeminal endings, and prostaglandin synthesis by **cyclo-oxygenase** are the targets.
migraine-drugs.mechanism: **CGRP** causes meningeal vasodilation and **neurogenic inflammation** and sensitises pain pathways, while prostaglandins further sensitise trigeminal nociceptors and amplify central pain transmission.
migraine-drugs.manifestation: This explains throbbing **headache**, **nausea**, photophobia and phonophobia, with pain worsened by movement because sensitised meningeal nociceptors respond to normal pulsation.
migraine-drugs.intervention: **Sumatriptan** activates 5-HT1B/1D receptors to constrict vessels and block mediator release, **gepants** and monoclonal antibodies block CGRP signalling, and NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis.
migraine-drugs.adverse: Triptans cause **chest tightness**, paraesthesia and vasoconstriction related effects, CGRP blockers mainly cause **constipation** and injection site reactions, and NSAIDs cause gastric irritation and renal effects.

migraine-pathophysiology.trigger: Attack triggers such as stress, **hormonal shifts** and missed **sleep** ignite a migraine in a sensitive **trigeminovascular system**.
migraine-pathophysiology.target: Targets are cortical **neurons**, the **trigeminal nerve** and meningeal **blood vessels** with **CGRP receptors**.
migraine-pathophysiology.mechanism: **Cortical spreading depression** sweeps aura symptoms while **trigeminal fibres** release **CGRP**, dilating vessels and driving **neurogenic inflammation**.
migraine-pathophysiology.manifestation: **Prodrome** with yawning and craving precedes visual **aura**, then throbbing **headache** with nausea and light **sensitivity**.
migraine-pathophysiology.intervention: **Triptans** constrict vessels and quiet nerve firing while **CGRP blockers** stop the peptide signal and **NSAIDs** ease inflammation.
migraine-pathophysiology.adverse: **Triptan** action causes chest tightness and **tingling** while **CGRP blockers** cause **constipation**.

mitral-regurgitation.trigger: Valve injury from prolapse, **ischaemia** or **endocarditis** prevents full leaflet closure at the start of systole.
mitral-regurgitation.target: Targets are the **mitral leaflets**, **left atrium** and **left ventricle** that together handle forward and backward flow.
mitral-regurgitation.mechanism: Systolic backflow through the **regurgitant orifice** volume loads the **left atrium** and **left ventricle**, which dilate over time.
mitral-regurgitation.manifestation: A blowing **holosystolic murmur** with **dyspnoea** and crackles reflects pulmonary congestion plus falling forward **cardiac output**.
mitral-regurgitation.intervention: **Vasodilators** ease forward flow and **diuretics** unload congestion while **valve repair** restores lasting leaflet closure.
mitral-regurgitation.adverse: **Diuretic** action causes **hypokalaemia** and volume depletion while vasodilators cause **hypotension** and renal strain from low perfusion.

mitral-stenosis.trigger: **Rheumatic carditis** heals with fusion of the **mitral valve** commissures and chordae, progressively narrowing the valve opening.
mitral-stenosis.target: The stenotic **mitral valve** obstructs flow from the **left atrium** to the left ventricle during diastole.
mitral-stenosis.mechanism: Left atrial pressure rises and the atrium dilates, transmitting pressure backward to cause **pulmonary congestion** and later **pulmonary hypertension** with right ventricular strain.
mitral-stenosis.manifestation: Exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea and haemoptysis reflect lung congestion, while atrial dilatation causes **atrial fibrillation** and systemic **embolism** from atrial thrombus.
mitral-stenosis.intervention: **Diuretics** reduce congestion, **beta blockers** slow heart rate to lengthen diastolic filling, and balloon valvotomy or valve replacement relieves the obstruction.
mitral-stenosis.adverse: **Beta blockers** can cause bradycardia and fatigue, diuretics can cause volume depletion and electrolyte loss, and **anticoagulation** increases bleeding risk.

mood-stabilisers-antipsychotics.trigger: A manic episode with overactive neuronal signalling and excess **dopamine** activity in **mesolimbic pathways** drives elevated mood and psychomotor pressure.
mood-stabilisers-antipsychotics.target: **IMPase and GSK-3**, voltage gated **sodium channels** and **D2 receptors** modulate inositol signalling, neuronal excitability and dopamine transmission.
mood-stabilisers-antipsychotics.mechanism: Lithium dampens **inositol signalling** and GSK-3 activity, anticonvulsants reduce repetitive **sodium channel** firing, and D2 blockade reduces **dopamine** effect in mesolimbic pathways.
mood-stabilisers-antipsychotics.manifestation: Overactivity explains **pressured speech**, **reduced need for sleep** and **grandiosity** with agitation, settling as neuronal excitability and dopamine signalling fall.
mood-stabilisers-antipsychotics.intervention: **Lithium** stabilises mood through inositol and GSK-3 pathways, **valproate** and carbamazepine reduce excitability, and **antipsychotics** block D2 receptors for acute mania.
mood-stabilisers-antipsychotics.adverse: Lithium causes **tremor**, polyuria and hypothyroidism, valproate causes weight gain and hepatic effects, carbamazepine causes hyponatraemia and rash, and D2 blockers cause **extrapyramidal effects**.

motor-neuron-disease.trigger: Age linked **gene** susceptibility plus **glutamate** excess and protein mishandling starts selective **motor neuron** death.
motor-neuron-disease.target: Targets are cortical **upper motor neurons**, spinal **lower motor neurons** and **bulbar** motor nuclei.
motor-neuron-disease.mechanism: **Glutamate excitotoxicity** overstimulates cells while misfolded **proteins** choke transport, so **motor neurons** waste without regrowth.
motor-neuron-disease.manifestation: Mixed wasting with **fasciculations** and weak **reflexes** plus stiff **spasticity** and brisk reflexes occur with spared **sensation**.
motor-neuron-disease.intervention: **Riluzole** calms excitotoxic drive to slow decline while **multidisciplinary support** and **ventilatory support** ease swallowing and breathing.
motor-neuron-disease.adverse: **Riluzole** action causes nausea, fatigue and **liver injury** while **ventilatory support** brings dry mouth, **aerophagia** and device dependence.

ms-immunotherapy.trigger: Autoreactive **T cells** and **B cells** cross into the central nervous system and drive relapsing inflammation and demyelination in multiple sclerosis.
ms-immunotherapy.target: **S1P receptors**, **alpha4 integrin**, **CD20** on B cells and peripheral immune balance control lymphocyte exit, brain entry and B cell survival.
ms-immunotherapy.mechanism: Lymphocytes leave lymph nodes through **S1P signalling**, adhere through **alpha4 integrin** to enter the brain, and B cells present antigen and release cytokines that amplify demyelination.
ms-immunotherapy.manifestation: Focal inflammation explains **relapses** with weakness, visual loss or sensory disturbance, and accumulating **demyelination** explains progressive disability between attacks.
ms-immunotherapy.intervention: **Fingolimod** traps lymphocytes in lymph nodes, **natalizumab** blocks alpha4 integrin entry, **ocrelizumab** depletes CD20 B cells, and interferon beta or glatiramer rebalance immune activity.
ms-immunotherapy.adverse: Trapping or blocking lymphocytes causes **infection**, natalizumab risks **progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy**, fingolimod causes bradycardia and lymphopenia, and anti-CD20 drugs cause infusion reactions and infection.

multiple-myeloma.trigger: A malignant clone of **plasma cells** expands in bone marrow, often evolving from **MGUS** through smouldering disease to active myeloma.
multiple-myeloma.target: Clonal plasma cells secrete a monoclonal **paraprotein** and excess **free light chains**, while marrow and bone signalling disturb osteoclast and osteoblast balance.
multiple-myeloma.mechanism: Light chains injure renal tubules, marrow replacement suppresses normal blood formation, and increased **osteoclast** activity with suppressed **osteoblasts** produces lytic bone lesions.
multiple-myeloma.manifestation: The **CRAB features** are hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, **anaemia** and bone pain or fractures, with infection risk from suppressed normal immunoglobulins.
multiple-myeloma.intervention: **Proteasome inhibitors** kill myeloma cells by blocking protein disposal, **bisphosphonates** reduce osteoclast bone damage, and supportive care treats kidney injury and anaemia.
multiple-myeloma.adverse: **Proteasome inhibitors** can cause **peripheral neuropathy** and thrombocytopenia, while bisphosphonates can cause kidney injury and osteonecrosis of the jaw.

multiple-sclerosis.trigger: In a genetically susceptible host, environmental factors activate **autoreactive T cells** and **B cells** against myelin. Activated cells cross the **blood brain barrier** to enter the central nervous system.
multiple-sclerosis.target: Immune attack targets **oligodendrocytes** and the **myelin sheath** around central axons. Inflammatory cytokines and antibodies strip myelin and injure the underlying axon.
multiple-sclerosis.mechanism: Demyelination slows or blocks **saltatory conduction**, forming a sclerotic **plaque** visible on imaging. Remyelination allows remission, but repeated attacks cause axonal loss and progressive disability.
multiple-sclerosis.manifestation: Optic neuritis, limb weakness and sensory disturbance reflect **conduction block** in affected tracts. **Relapses** separated by remission, later becoming **progression**, mirror new plaques and accumulated axonal injury.
multiple-sclerosis.intervention: **Glucocorticoids** shorten relapses by suppressing inflammation and restoring the **blood brain barrier**. **Disease modifying therapies** reduce relapse frequency by trapping lymphocytes or depleting B cells.
multiple-sclerosis.adverse: **Glucocorticoids** cause hyperglycaemia, insomnia and infection risk from broad **immunosuppression**. **Disease modifying therapies** increase infection risk and can cause liver injury because they alter immune surveillance.

muscarinic.trigger: Increased **parasympathetic drive** releases **acetylcholine** from nerve terminals, while drugs or toxins may mimic or prolong this signal.
muscarinic.target: The signal acts on **M2 receptors** in the heart and **M3 receptors** in smooth muscle, glands and the eye.
muscarinic.mechanism: **M2 receptors** use **G alpha i** to reduce cyclic AMP and slow pacemaker activity. **M3 receptors** use **G alpha q** to raise calcium and drive contraction and secretion.
muscarinic.manifestation: Excess signalling causes a **slow pulse**, **bronchoconstriction**, gut cramps, salivation and a small pupil. Blockade causes the opposite pattern with a fast pulse, dry mouth and urinary retention.
muscarinic.intervention: **Atropine** and related antimuscarinics block the receptors, while **cholinesterase inhibitors** raise acetylcholine. Direct agonists such as **bethanechol** activate receptors without needing nerve release.
muscarinic.adverse: **Atropine** blockade produces dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention and confusion. Excess **cholinesterase inhibitor** action causes vomiting, diarrhoea, bradycardia and bronchospasm.

muscle-contraction.trigger: A motor nerve impulse releases **acetylcholine** at the **neuromuscular junction**, triggering a muscle fibre action potential.
muscle-contraction.target: **Nicotinic receptors**, **ryanodine receptors** and **troponin** link excitation to calcium release and actin exposure.
muscle-contraction.mechanism: Calcium binds **troponin**, moving **tropomyosin** from actin sites so **myosin cross bridges** cycle using ATP and shorten the sarcomere.
muscle-contraction.manifestation: Coordinated cross bridge cycling produces **muscle contraction**, while absent ATP after death leaves bridges attached in **rigor mortis** and metabolic depletion causes **fatigue**.
muscle-contraction.intervention: A **neuromuscular blocker** prevents acetylcholine action and paralyses muscle, whereas a **cholinesterase inhibitor** raises acetylcholine and prolongs its effect.
muscle-contraction.adverse: Excess **acetylcholine** from a **cholinesterase inhibitor** causes salivation, gut cramps, miosis and **bronchospasm** through muscarinic stimulation.

myasthenia-gravis.trigger: Autoimmunity, often linked to the **thymus**, produces **anti acetylcholine receptor antibodies** in most patients with generalised disease.
myasthenia-gravis.target: Antibodies bind **acetylcholine receptors** at the postsynaptic membrane of the **neuromuscular junction**, reducing receptors available for nerve signalling.
myasthenia-gravis.mechanism: Receptor blockade, internalisation and **complement** mediated membrane damage lower the **endplate potential**, so repeated activity causes fading muscle contraction.
myasthenia-gravis.manifestation: Fatigable weakness causes **ptosis**, diplopia and dysarthria, and spread to limb, bulbar and **respiratory muscles** can produce myasthenic crisis.
myasthenia-gravis.intervention: **Cholinesterase inhibitors** prolong acetylcholine action, **immunosuppression** reduces antibody production, and thymectomy or plasmapheresis helps selected severe disease.
myasthenia-gravis.adverse: **Cholinesterase inhibitors** can cause diarrhoea, cramps and excess secretions from increased **acetylcholine**, while immunosuppression increases infection and metabolic complications.

neonatal-jaundice.trigger: Rapid **red cell** turnover after birth plus immature **liver conjugation** creates bilirubin faster than the newborn can clear it.
neonatal-jaundice.target: Targets are **hepatocytes** using **UGT enzyme** for conjugation and **albumin** that carries unconjugated bilirubin in blood.
neonatal-jaundice.mechanism: Unconjugated **bilirubin** builds up in **blood**, deposits in skin and, when free, crosses the **blood brain barrier**.
neonatal-jaundice.manifestation: Yellow **skin** and **sclera** progress downward with poor feeding while severe disease causes **lethargy** and kernicterus injury.
neonatal-jaundice.intervention: **Phototherapy** converts skin **bilirubin** to excretable forms while **feeding** and fluids promote gut clearance of pigment.
neonatal-jaundice.adverse: **Exchange transfusion** removes bilirubin fast but risks **infection**, **electrolyte shifts** and vessel injury from the procedure itself.

neonatal-respiratory-distress-surfactant.trigger: Very **preterm birth** before **type II pneumocytes** mature leaves the lung without enough surfactant for air breathing.
neonatal-respiratory-distress-surfactant.target: The target is the **alveolus** lined by **surfactant** film at the **air fluid** interface beside lung capillaries.
neonatal-respiratory-distress-surfactant.mechanism: Missing surfactant raises **surface tension** so **alveoli** collapse, form **hyaline membranes** and shunt blood past unventilated units.
neonatal-respiratory-distress-surfactant.manifestation: **Tachypnoea**, grunting and **hypoxia** develop with a ground glass **chest film** reflecting widespread collapse and edema.
neonatal-respiratory-distress-surfactant.intervention: **Antenatal steroid** speeds lung maturation while postnatal **surfactant** plus **CPAP** hold alveoli open for gas exchange.
neonatal-respiratory-distress-surfactant.adverse: **CPAP** pressure can cause **pneumothorax** and nasal injury while excess **oxygen** risks eye and lung damage in preterms.

nephron-aki.trigger: Falling perfusion, direct tubular or glomerular injury, or blocked outflow triggers **acute kidney injury** by reducing filtration or damaging the **nephron**.
nephron-aki.target: Injury affects the **glomerulus**, **tubules**, interstitium or urinary outflow tract depending on the underlying cause.
nephron-aki.mechanism: **Prerenal failure** lowers filtration pressure, **acute tubular injury** causes cell death and cast obstruction, and **postrenal obstruction** raises tubular pressure until filtration stops.
nephron-aki.manifestation: Rising waste products, **oliguria**, fluid overload and potassium and acid retention follow falling filtration. **Nephritic syndrome** gives blood in urine, while **nephrotic syndrome** gives heavy protein loss and oedema.
nephron-aki.intervention: **Intravenous fluids** restore perfusion in prerenal injury, **relief of obstruction** treats postrenal failure, and stopping **nephrotoxins** or giving steroids for immune injury removes the cause.
nephron-aki.adverse: Excess **fluids** in established failure cause **pulmonary oedema**, while **steroids** raise glucose and infection risk by suppressing immune and metabolic control.

nephrotic-syndrome.trigger: Immune injury to **podocytes** in minimal change, **FSGS** or membranous disease disrupts the filtration barrier. Increased permeability starts protein loss across the **glomerulus**.
nephrotic-syndrome.target: The target is the **glomerular filter** with its **podocytes**, basement membrane and endothelium. Damaged foot processes lose selectivity and leak **albumin**.
nephrotic-syndrome.mechanism: **Podocyte** effacement widens filtration slits so **albumin** leaks into urine in large amounts. Low oncotic pressure shifts fluid out while the liver raises **lipoprotein** synthesis.
nephrotic-syndrome.manifestation: Heavy proteinuria causes **oedema** around the eyes and legs with low albumin. Lost anticoagulants invite **thrombosis** while antibody loss invites **infection**.
nephrotic-syndrome.intervention: **Steroid** therapy suppresses immune **podocyte** injury and reduces protein leak in responsive disease. **ACE inhibitor** drugs lower pressure inside the **glomerulus** and ease proteinuria.
nephrotic-syndrome.adverse: **Steroid** therapy raises **glucose**, weight and infection risk through systemic immunosuppression. **ACE inhibitor** drugs may cause dry cough with **hyperkalaemia** through vascular and hormonal effects.

neuromuscular-blockers.trigger: Surgery or ventilation requires controlled **muscle paralysis** and abolition of reflex movement. Anaesthesia alone may not prevent movement at the **neuromuscular junction**.
neuromuscular-blockers.target: Postsynaptic **nicotinic receptors** at the muscle end plate and breakdown by **acetylcholinesterase** control transmission. **Suxamethonium** and competitive blockers act at the receptor.
neuromuscular-blockers.mechanism: Competitive blockers occupy **nicotinic receptors** without opening them, while **suxamethonium** opens the channel persistently and makes the end plate inexcitable. Both prevent effective **muscle contraction**.
neuromuscular-blockers.manifestation: Blockade produces flaccid paralysis, absent breathing effort, and inability to protect the **airway**. Recovery follows drug clearance or reversal and return of **train of four** responses.
neuromuscular-blockers.intervention: **Neostigmine** inhibits acetylcholinesterase to raise acetylcholine and compete off competitive blockers, while **sugammadex** encapsulates rocuronium type drugs. Ventilation is maintained until strength returns.
neuromuscular-blockers.adverse: **Suxamethonium** can cause hyperkalaemia, muscle pain, and malignant hyperthermia in susceptible patients. **Neostigmine** excess causes bradycardia, salivation, and bronchospasm from widespread **muscarinic** effects.

nitrates-pde5-vasodilators.trigger: Angina, erectile dysfunction or pulmonary hypertension reflects inadequate **nitric oxide** signalling or excessive **vascular smooth muscle** tone needing vasodilation.
nitrates-pde5-vasodilators.target: **Soluble guanylyl cyclase**, **phosphodiesterase type 5** and **potassium channels** in vascular smooth muscle control cGMP levels and membrane potential.
nitrates-pde5-vasodilators.mechanism: Nitric oxide raises **cGMP**, cGMP lowers intracellular calcium and relaxes muscle, **PDE5** breaks cGMP down, and potassium channel opening hyperpolarises the cell.
nitrates-pde5-vasodilators.manifestation: Increased tone explains **angina** from coronary supply demand mismatch and **erectile dysfunction** from poor penile blood flow, with raised pressure in pulmonary vessels.
nitrates-pde5-vasodilators.intervention: **Glyceryl trinitrate** donates nitric oxide, **sildenafil** inhibits PDE5, and **nicorandil** or **minoxidil** opens potassium channels to dilate vessels.
nitrates-pde5-vasodilators.adverse: Vasodilation causes **headache**, **flushing** and **postural hypotension**, and combining nitrates with PDE5 inhibitors can cause dangerous profound hypotension.

nsaids-steroids.trigger: **Tissue injury** or **inflammation** starts the process, as damaged membranes release substrate for mediator production that drives pain, fever, and swelling.
nsaids-steroids.target: The targets are **phospholipase A2** upstream and the **COX-1** and **COX-2** enzymes downstream, which convert arachidonic acid to prostanoids and related mediators.
nsaids-steroids.mechanism: **Phospholipase A2** releases **arachidonic acid**, then **COX enzymes** make inflammatory prostaglandins while the lipoxygenase route makes **leukotrienes** that narrow airways and amplify inflammation.
nsaids-steroids.manifestation: Inflammatory **prostaglandins** produce **pain**, **fever**, and **swelling**, while protective prostanoids normally defend the stomach lining, kidney perfusion, and platelet function.
nsaids-steroids.intervention: **Corticosteroids** block phospholipase A2, **aspirin** and other **NSAIDs** block COX enzymes, and **celecoxib** type drugs preferentially block COX-2.
nsaids-steroids.adverse: Blocking protective **COX-1** products causes **gastric ulceration**, bleeding, and reduced **kidney perfusion**, while **corticosteroids** cause hyperglycaemia, hypertension, and immune suppression through widespread gene effects.

obesity-adipose-pathogenesis.trigger: Chronic **energy surplus** from excess intake over expenditure starts fat gain. Sedentary **lifestyle pattern** plus easy calories keeps the surplus going.
obesity-adipose-pathogenesis.target: Enlarging **adipocytes** are the core target with **leptin signalling** to the brain. Liver, muscle and **pancreatic islets** suffer the spillover effects.
obesity-adipose-pathogenesis.mechanism: Stuffed **adipocytes** leak **fatty acids** and resist **leptin signals** so hunger persists. Recruited **macrophages** release cytokines that block insulin action.
obesity-adipose-pathogenesis.manifestation: **Insulin resistance** raises glucose toward **type 2 diabetes** while fat in liver causes **fatty liver**. Together they form **metabolic syndrome** with hypertension and dyslipidaemia.
obesity-adipose-pathogenesis.intervention: Sustained **lifestyle change** with diet and activity shrinks fat stores first. **GLP-1 based drug** therapy curbs appetite while **bariatric surgery** restricts intake durably.
obesity-adipose-pathogenesis.adverse: **GLP-1 based drugs** slow **gastric emptying** so nausea, vomiting and fullness follow. Rapid loss after **bariatric surgery** can add gallstones and nutrient gaps.

obstructive-sleep-apnoea.trigger: Sleep onset relaxes **pharyngeal dilator muscles** in a crowded **upper airway** shaped by obesity and anatomy. This sleep related loss of tone sets the stage for collapse.
obstructive-sleep-apnoea.target: The targets are the **pharyngeal dilator muscles**, the collapsible **upper airway** wall and the **carotid chemoreceptors** sensing oxygen. Lungs, blood and the heart feel the downstream strain.
obstructive-sleep-apnoea.mechanism: Loss of **dilator tone** lets negative inspiratory pressure suck the **upper airway** shut and cause **apnoea**. Repeated apnoeas drop oxygen and trigger brief **arousals** with surging sympathetic drive.
obstructive-sleep-apnoea.manifestation: Fragmented sleep causes daytime **sleepiness** with poor concentration and morning **headache**. Nightly **hypoxia** plus surges drive **hypertension** and strain the failing heart.
obstructive-sleep-apnoea.intervention: Side sleeping and **weight loss** reduce crowding and collapse in mild disease. **CPAP** splints the airway open while a **mandibular device** or surgery widens it.
obstructive-sleep-apnoea.adverse: Pressurised **CPAP** air dries the **nasal mucosa** and mask pressure irritates facial skin. Poor fit then causes leak, noise and broken **sleep quality** that defeats therapy.

oncogenes-tumour-suppressors.trigger: Accumulated **mutations** from **carcinogens**, replication errors or inherited defects activate growth pathways and disable genomic guardians over time.
oncogenes-tumour-suppressors.target: Proto-oncogenes such as **RAS** drive proliferation, while tumour suppressors including **TP53** and **RB** enforce checkpoints, repair and apoptosis.
oncogenes-tumour-suppressors.mechanism: Gain of function in **oncogenes** accelerates growth signalling, and loss of **tumour suppressors** permits survival and division of genetically damaged cells.
oncogenes-tumour-suppressors.manifestation: Progressive multi-hit change produces uncontrolled growth, **invasion** and **metastasis**, as malignant cells evade **apoptosis** and immune destruction.
oncogenes-tumour-suppressors.intervention: **Targeted kinase inhibitors** block abnormal growth signalling, while **chemotherapy** preferentially injures rapidly dividing cells with damaged repair capacity.
oncogenes-tumour-suppressors.adverse: **Kinase inhibitors** can injure normal signalling in skin, gut and heart, while **chemotherapy** causes **myelosuppression**, nausea and infection through effects on dividing healthy cells.

opioid-pain-pathway.trigger: Tissue injury or inflammation activates peripheral **nociceptors** and releases **prostaglandins** that lower their firing threshold.
opioid-pain-pathway.target: Signals travel via **dorsal horn** synapses and the **spinothalamic tract** to thalamus and cortex, while descending pathways modulate transmission.
opioid-pain-pathway.mechanism: **Glutamate** and **substance P** transmit nociceptive signals across the dorsal horn, and repeated input increases central sensitivity. Descending **serotonin** and **noradrenaline** pathways normally dampen this transmission.
opioid-pain-pathway.manifestation: Ascending activity produces localised **pain perception** with tenderness and guarding, while central sensitisation causes **hyperalgesia** and pain from light touch.
opioid-pain-pathway.intervention: **NSAIDs** reduce prostaglandin sensitisation in the periphery, **opioids** act on spinal and brain receptors to reduce transmission, and **local anaesthetics** block nerve conduction.
opioid-pain-pathway.adverse: **Opioids** depress brainstem respiratory drive and slow gut motility, causing **respiratory depression**, **constipation**, sedation and dependence with continued use.

opioids.trigger: **Pain** signals and endogenous **opioid peptides** start the process, as the nervous system uses inhibitory signalling to limit pain transmission and control breathing drive.
opioids.target: The target is the **mu opioid receptor**, a **Gi coupled receptor** on pain pathway neurons and on respiratory neurons in the brainstem.
opioids.mechanism: **Mu receptor** activation inhibits **adenylyl cyclase**, lowers **cyclic AMP**, reduces calcium entry and transmitter release, and opens potassium channels to hyperpolarise the neuron.
opioids.manifestation: Reduced **pain transmission** produces analgesia and calm, while reduced **respiratory drive** slows breathing, and gut and pupil effects produce constipation and **miosis**.
opioids.intervention: **Morphine** and **fentanyl** type full agonists maximise mu signalling for severe pain, **buprenorphine** is a partial agonist, and **naloxone** competitively reverses agonist effects in overdose.
opioids.adverse: Full **mu agonists** cause **respiratory depression**, sedation, nausea, and **constipation** from the same receptor action, while **naloxone** can precipitate acute withdrawal in dependent patients.

organophosphate-poisoning.trigger: Exposure to an **organophosphate insecticide** through skin, inhalation or ingestion starts poisoning. Severity rises with amount absorbed and speed of **enzyme inhibition**.
organophosphate-poisoning.target: The compound irreversibly inhibits **acetylcholinesterase** in synapses and on red cells. **Acetylcholine** then accumulates at muscarinic, nicotinic and central synapses.
organophosphate-poisoning.mechanism: Excess **acetylcholine** overstimulates **muscarinic receptors** causing secretions and bronchospasm, and **nicotinic receptors** causing fasciculations then paralysis. Central overstimulation causes confusion, seizures and respiratory depression.
organophosphate-poisoning.manifestation: The **SLUDGE signs** of salivation, lacrimation, urination, defaecation and miosis reflect muscarinic excess. **Fasciculations**, weakness and **respiratory failure** reflect nicotinic and central involvement.
organophosphate-poisoning.intervention: **Atropine** blocks muscarinic receptors to dry secretions and relieve bronchospasm. An **oxime** such as pralidoxime reactivates **acetylcholinesterase** before ageing, restoring neuromuscular function.
organophosphate-poisoning.adverse: **Atropine** causes dry mouth, tachycardia and urinary retention because it blocks **muscarinic receptors** widely. **Oximes** can cause transient weakness and dizziness, and they fail once the enzyme has aged.

osteomyelitis.trigger: **Bacteraemia** from skin or nearby infection seeds bone through blood. Trauma or **immune suppression** helps organisms lodge and grow.
osteomyelitis.target: Metaphyseal **bone marrow** with slow flow, lifting **periosteum** and starved **cortical bone** are the targets.
osteomyelitis.mechanism: Bacteria grow in **metaphysis** and form **pus under pressure** inside rigid bone. Dead **sequestrum** separates while new **involucrum** shells around it.
osteomyelitis.manifestation: Pressure causes severe **bone pain** with fever, limp and refusal to bear weight. Chronic disease forms a draining **skin sinus** and weak bone prone to **pathological fracture**.
osteomyelitis.intervention: Prolonged **antibiotics** kill bacteria in bone and blood over weeks. Timely **surgical debridement** plus **immobilisation** removes dead bone and rests healing.
osteomyelitis.adverse: Long **antibiotics** cause gut upset and **drug rash** from hypersensitivity reactions. Surgery adds risk of **wound infection** with delayed healing and stiffness.

osteoporosis-bone-remodelling.trigger: Ageing, **oestrogen deficiency** after menopause, **immobility** and poor nutrition shift normal remodelling toward net bone loss.
osteoporosis-bone-remodelling.target: **Osteoclasts** resorb bone while **osteoblasts** form it, controlled by **RANKL** from osteoblast lineage cells and its decoy receptor **osteoprotegerin**.
osteoporosis-bone-remodelling.mechanism: Oestrogen loss raises **RANKL** signalling and osteoclast survival, so resorption outpaces formation by **osteoblasts** and trabeculae thin and perforate.
osteoporosis-bone-remodelling.manifestation: Loss of **trabecular bone** and cortical thinning weaken the skeleton, causing height loss, kyphosis and **fragility fractures** of vertebra, hip and wrist.
osteoporosis-bone-remodelling.intervention: **Bisphosphonates** bind bone and impair osteoclasts, **calcium** and **vitamin D** correct deficiency, and anabolic agents stimulate osteoblast formation.
osteoporosis-bone-remodelling.adverse: **Bisphosphonates** can irritate the oesophagus and rarely cause **osteonecrosis of the jaw**, while excess calcium and vitamin D can cause hypercalcaemia.

oxygen-haemoglobin-dissociation-curve.trigger: Rising tissue **oxygen demand** during exercise, fever or anaemia calls for more unloading. Efficient lung **oxygen loading** must still fill haemoglobin fully.
oxygen-haemoglobin-dissociation-curve.target: The **haemoglobin tetramer** in **red cells**, its binding **haem groups** and tuning **hydrogen ions** are the targets.
oxygen-haemoglobin-dissociation-curve.mechanism: Cooperative **oxygen binding** steepens the sigmoid curve around **P50**. Rising **hydrogen ions** and carbon dioxide loosen affinity through the **Bohr effect**.
oxygen-haemoglobin-dissociation-curve.manifestation: Right shift aids **tissue unloading** but impairs **lung loading** at altitude or anaemia. Left shift holds oxygen tightly and starves tissues despite high **oxygen saturation**.
oxygen-haemoglobin-dissociation-curve.intervention: **Acid base correction** plus fever control and **oxygen therapy** restores normal affinity and loading. Transfusion improves **oxygen delivery** when anaemia limits carriage.
oxygen-haemoglobin-dissociation-curve.adverse: Excess **oxygen therapy** suppresses drive in carbon dioxide retainers and causes **hypercapnia**. Overtransfusion risks **volume overload** with breathlessness from raised pressures.

paracetamol-mechanism-nac-rescue.trigger: Pain or fever creates **prostaglandin** demand in **central pathways**, the clinical problem **paracetamol** treats.
paracetamol-mechanism-nac-rescue.target: **Central COX enzymes** with **TRPV1** and **cannabinoid pathways** via **AM404** set pain and temperature control.
paracetamol-mechanism-nac-rescue.mechanism: **Paracetamol** limits central **prostaglandin synthesis** and forms **AM404** to strengthen descending inhibition and lower the set point.
paracetamol-mechanism-nac-rescue.manifestation: Pain eases and **fever** falls without platelet block, while overdose causes **hepatic necrosis** with **transaminitis** and coagulopathy.
paracetamol-mechanism-nac-rescue.intervention: **N-acetylcysteine** restores **glutathione** to detoxify **NAPQI**, with early **charcoal** limiting absorption after overdose.
paracetamol-mechanism-nac-rescue.adverse: Even therapeutic use risks **hepatotoxicity** in **glutathione depletion**, and **N-acetylcysteine** can cause **flushing** with wheeze.

paracetamol-toxicity.trigger: Taking **paracetamol** beyond safe handling capacity, usually in **overdose**, saturates the normal conjugation routes in the **liver**.
paracetamol-toxicity.target: Minor oxidation produces **NAPQI**, normally detoxified by hepatic **glutathione** within **hepatocytes** around the central vein.
paracetamol-toxicity.mechanism: When sulphation and **glucuronidation** saturate, more **NAPQI** forms, **glutathione** is depleted, and NAPQI binds hepatocyte proteins causing oxidative injury.
paracetamol-toxicity.manifestation: Centrilobular **necrosis** causes rising liver injury, **coagulopathy** and encephalopathy, progressing to acute **liver failure** when injury is extensive.
paracetamol-toxicity.intervention: Early **activated charcoal** reduces absorption, **N-acetylcysteine** replenishes glutathione and detoxifies NAPQI, and **transplantation** replaces a failing liver.
paracetamol-toxicity.adverse: **N-acetylcysteine** can cause flushing, urticaria and bronchospasm through **anaphylactoid reactions**, while **charcoal** risks aspiration if the airway is unprotected.

parkinson-basal-ganglia.trigger: Progressive loss of **dopaminergic neurons** in the **substantia nigra pars compacta** starts the disease, with Lewy pathology spreading over years. Ageing and genetic susceptibility contribute.
parkinson-basal-ganglia.target: Dopamine normally modulates the **direct pathway** and **indirect pathway** through striatal receptors. Its loss alters output from the **globus pallidus interna** to the thalamus.
parkinson-basal-ganglia.mechanism: Reduced dopamine weakens the **direct pathway** and overactivates the **indirect pathway**, increasing inhibitory output from the **globus pallidus interna**. The thalamus is over inhibited, so cortical movement drive falls.
parkinson-basal-ganglia.manifestation: **Bradykinesia** with rigidity and resting tremor reflects failure to scale movement from excessive **basal ganglia** inhibition. Gait freezing and small handwriting show impaired initiation and amplitude of movement.
parkinson-basal-ganglia.intervention: **Levodopa** crosses into brain and is converted to dopamine, while **dopamine agonists** directly stimulate receptors. **MAO B inhibitors** and COMT inhibitors prolong dopamine action.
parkinson-basal-ganglia.adverse: **Levodopa** causes dyskinesias and motor fluctuations from pulsatile **dopamine receptor** stimulation. **Dopamine agonists** cause nausea, hallucinations and impulse control disorders through limbic dopamine activation.

pelvic-inflammatory-disease.trigger: Untreated cervical **chlamydia** or **gonorrhoea** ascends after menstruation or instrumentation through the open **cervical canal**.
pelvic-inflammatory-disease.target: Bacteria infect columnar **endocervical cells**, then spread to the **fallopian tubes** and pelvic **peritoneum** around the ovaries.
pelvic-inflammatory-disease.mechanism: Bacterial invasion triggers neutrophil **salpingitis** with purulent **exudate** and fibrin **adhesions** that block tubal **cilia**.
pelvic-inflammatory-disease.manifestation: Tubal inflammation causes pelvic **pain** with fever and vaginal **discharge**, while scarring causes **infertility** and ectopic **pregnancy**.
pelvic-inflammatory-disease.intervention: Broad spectrum **antibiotics** clear cervical and tubal **pathogens** while image guided **drainage** removes persistent **abscess**.
pelvic-inflammatory-disease.adverse: **Antibiotics** can cause **nausea** with diarrhoea from gut disturbance while **doxycycline** may cause light sensitive **rash**.

peptic-ulcer.trigger: **Helicobacter pylori** infection or **NSAID** use weakens mucosal defence and allows acid injury to begin.
peptic-ulcer.target: The gastric and duodenal mucosa loses its **mucus bicarbonate barrier** and **prostaglandin** mediated protection and blood flow.
peptic-ulcer.mechanism: **Hydrochloric acid** and **pepsin** erode through epithelium into submucosa, forming a crater that can reach vessels or the serosa.
peptic-ulcer.manifestation: Mucosal erosion causes burning **epigastric pain**, while vessel erosion causes **haematemesis** or melaena and full thickness breach causes **perforation** with peritonitis.
peptic-ulcer.intervention: **Proton pump inhibitors** suppress acid secretion, **antibiotic eradication therapy** clears Helicobacter pylori, and stopping the offending NSAID restores defence.
peptic-ulcer.adverse: **Proton pump inhibitors** reduce acid dependent absorption and alter gut flora, predisposing to **hypomagnesaemia**, enteric infection and rebound acid hypersecretion.

pericarditis.trigger: **Viral infection**, **myocardial infarction** or **autoimmune disease** triggers acute inflammation of the pericardial layers.
pericarditis.target: **Parietal pericardium** and **visceral pericardium** with adjacent **epicardial surface** are the inflamed targets.
pericarditis.mechanism: **Inflammatory cells** and **fibrin exudate** roughen the layers so they rub, leak fluid and later form a stiff **fibrous shell**.
pericarditis.manifestation: **Pleuritic chest pain** and **pericardial friction rub** mark inflammation, with **diffuse ST elevation** and tamponade when effusion compresses.
pericarditis.intervention: **Anti-inflammatory treatment** and **colchicine** dampen inflammation, while **pericardial drainage** relieves tamponade compression.
pericarditis.adverse: **Anti-inflammatory drugs** can cause **gastric irritation** and **renal injury**, while colchicine commonly causes **diarrhoea** and cramps.

phaeochromocytoma.trigger: **Adrenal chromaffin tumour** episodically releases excess **adrenaline** and **noradrenaline** during spells.
phaeochromocytoma.target: **Alpha1 receptors** on vessels and **beta1 receptors** on heart mediate constriction and cardiac stimulation.
phaeochromocytoma.mechanism: **Catecholamine surge** constricts vessels and drives **heart rate** and contractility upward, spiking pressure in **paroxysms**.
phaeochromocytoma.manifestation: **Paroxysmal hypertension** with **palpitations** and sweating plus headache reflects episodic alpha and beta stimulation.
phaeochromocytoma.intervention: **Alpha blockade** comes first to open vessels, then **beta blockade** controls rhythm, followed by **tumour removal** after preparation.
phaeochromocytoma.adverse: **Alpha blockers** cause **postural hypotension** and **nasal congestion** through systemic vasodilatation and mucosal vessel relaxation.

pharmacokinetics-adme.trigger: Administration of a **drug** by oral or intravenous route triggers processes that determine **plasma concentration** over time.
pharmacokinetics-adme.target: **Plasma proteins**, hepatic **cytochrome enzymes** and renal excretion pathways govern free drug, clearance and duration.
pharmacokinetics-adme.mechanism: Unbound drug crosses membranes and reaches tissues, liver enzymes convert it to metabolites, and kidney or bile removes it, producing **half life** and **steady state**.
pharmacokinetics-adme.manifestation: Impaired **liver function** slows metabolism and impaired **kidney function** slows excretion, causing drug accumulation, toxicity or prolonged **therapeutic effect**.
pharmacokinetics-adme.intervention: An **enzyme inducer** accelerates metabolism and lowers exposure, whereas an **enzyme inhibitor** raises exposure and prolongs action.
pharmacokinetics-adme.adverse: An **enzyme inhibitor** raising drug levels can cause **toxicity**, while an **enzyme inducer** lowering levels can cause loss of efficacy and treatment failure.

pituitary-disorders.trigger: A benign **pituitary adenoma** autonomously secretes prolactin or **growth hormone**, while larger lesions compress normal tissue. Destructive injury then causes lasting **hypopituitarism**.
pituitary-disorders.target: Targets are lactotroph and somatotroph **pituitary cells**, peripheral **hormone receptors** and the nearby **optic chiasm**. Excess or deficient signalling reshapes growth and reproduction.
pituitary-disorders.mechanism: Unregulated **prolactin** suppresses gonadotrophins while excess **growth hormone** raises **insulin like growth factor** and tissue growth. Tumour pressure impairs residual **pituitary** function.
pituitary-disorders.manifestation: **Galactorrhoea** with infertility marks prolactin excess while enlarged hands and jaw mark **acromegaly**. Chiasmal compression causes **bitemporal hemianopia** with fatigue from hormone failure.
pituitary-disorders.intervention: **Dopamine agonist** drugs shrink prolactinomas through lactotroph **dopamine receptors**. **Somatostatin analogue** drugs or surgery curb **growth hormone** excess in acromegaly.
pituitary-disorders.adverse: **Dopamine agonist** drugs may cause nausea, postural **hypotension** and impulse changes through central effects. **Somatostatin analogue** drugs may cause gallstones with **hyperglycaemia** through gut hormone blockade.

pleural-effusion.trigger: Heart failure, pneumonia, malignancy or inflammation alters **Starling forces** or pleural permeability and increases fluid formation by **pleural capillaries**.
pleural-effusion.target: Fluid accumulates between visceral and parietal **pleura**, compressing adjacent **lung tissue** and restricting expansion of the **chest wall**.
pleural-effusion.mechanism: Raised hydrostatic pressure produces protein poor **transudate**, while increased permeability from inflammation produces protein rich **exudate** that separates pleural surfaces.
pleural-effusion.manifestation: Effusion causes **breathlessness** and pleuritic pain, with **dullness to percussion** and reduced **breath sounds** over the fluid.
pleural-effusion.intervention: Treating the cause reduces formation, while **thoracentesis** or a **chest drain** removes fluid, and **pleurodesis** seals the pleural space against recurrence.
pleural-effusion.adverse: Drainage can cause **pneumothorax**, bleeding and pain, and rapid removal may rarely cause **re expansion pulmonary oedema**.

pneumonia.trigger: Inhaled or aspirated **bacteria** reach the **alveoli** and overcome local defence, often after a viral illness or impaired clearance. Severity rises with organism virulence and poor host reserve.
pneumonia.target: Infection centres on the **alveoli** and surrounding interstitium of a lobe or segment. The key responding cells are **macrophages** and recruited neutrophils.
pneumonia.mechanism: **Neutrophil exudate**, fibrin and red cells fill air spaces to produce **consolidation** and red hepatisation. Filled alveoli cannot exchange gas, so blood passing them leaves with **low oxygen**.
pneumonia.manifestation: Patients develop **fever**, cough, purulent sputum, pleuritic pain and **breathlessness** with crackles over the affected lobe. Severe disease causes hypoxaemia, confusion and spread to the pleura as effusion or empyema.
pneumonia.intervention: An **antibiotic** treats the infection while **oxygen** supports gas exchange until consolidation clears. Using both together addresses cause and consequence in moderate to severe **pneumonia**.
pneumonia.adverse: **Antibiotics** can cause allergy, diarrhoea and Clostridioides difficile infection. **Oxygen** alone without antibiotics leaves the infection progressing, and excess oxygen can mask worsening ventilation.

pneumothorax.trigger: Air enters the pleural space through a ruptured **bleb**, injured chest wall or diseased **lung tissue**, breaking the normal pleural seal.
pneumothorax.target: Pleural air separates visceral and parietal **pleura**, abolishes negative **intrapleural pressure** and allows elastic recoil to collapse the **lung**.
pneumothorax.mechanism: In tension pneumothorax a **one way valve** traps air with each breath, raising pressure, shifting the **mediastinum** and compressing the **vena cava**.
pneumothorax.manifestation: Patients develop sudden **chest pain** and **breathlessness**, with hyperresonance and absent breath sounds, while tension causes **hypotension** and distended neck veins.
pneumothorax.intervention: Small cases may be observed, while tension needs immediate **needle decompression** followed by a **chest drain** to remove air and re expand lung.
pneumothorax.adverse: Needle or drain insertion can injure **intercostal vessels**, lung or nerves, causing **bleeding**, infection and persistent **air leak**.

poliomyelitis.trigger: Faecal oral ingestion of **poliovirus** in contaminated water or food reaches the unvaccinated gut without protective **vaccine immunity**.
poliomyelitis.target: Virus replicates in gut **lymphoid tissue**, then spreads in blood to spinal **anterior horn neurons** and brainstem **motor nuclei**.
poliomyelitis.mechanism: Virus invades **motor neurons** and halts protein synthesis, causing neuronal **necrosis** with loss of lower **motor units** and denervated **muscle fibres**.
poliomyelitis.manifestation: Neuron loss causes asymmetric flaccid **paralysis** with absent **reflexes**, while bulbar disease causes dysphagia with breathing **failure**.
poliomyelitis.intervention: **Vaccine** builds protective **antibodies** that block gut invasion while **ventilation** supports weak **respiratory muscles** during acute paralysis.
poliomyelitis.adverse: Injected **vaccine** may cause local **pain** with brief **fever** from immune response, while oral vaccine very rarely causes vaccine associated **paralysis**.

polycystic-kidney-disease.trigger: **PKD1 mutation** or **PKD2 mutation** impairs ciliary signalling and sets lifelong cyst formation in motion.
polycystic-kidney-disease.target: **Renal tubular cells** and **primary cilia** with defective **polycystin proteins** drive abnormal growth.
polycystic-kidney-disease.mechanism: **Tubular proliferation** plus **fluid secretion** expands cysts that compress and replace working **nephrons**.
polycystic-kidney-disease.manifestation: **Flank pain** and **haematuria** with **hypertension** and enlarging kidneys progress toward **kidney failure**.
polycystic-kidney-disease.intervention: **Blood pressure control** protects remaining nephrons and **tolvaptan** slows cyst growth, with **dialysis or transplant** for failure.
polycystic-kidney-disease.adverse: **Tolvaptan** blocks **vasopressin receptors** so **aquaresis** causes marked thirst and large volume dilute urine.

polycystic-ovary-syndrome.trigger: **Insulin resistance** with compensatory hyperinsulinaemia plus rapid **LH pulses** overstimulates the ovary in susceptible women.
polycystic-ovary-syndrome.target: Targets are ovarian **theca cells**, **granulosa cells** and **insulin receptors** that together control androgen and follicle growth.
polycystic-ovary-syndrome.mechanism: Excess **LH** and **insulin** raise thecal **androgens** which arrest follicles and block dominant follicle selection and ovulation.
polycystic-ovary-syndrome.manifestation: **Anovulation** causes irregular menses and subfertility while androgens cause **hirsutism**, acne and scalp **hair loss**.
polycystic-ovary-syndrome.intervention: **Lifestyle** and weight loss restore ovulation while **metformin** improves insulin sensitivity and cyclic **progestogen** protects the endometrium.
polycystic-ovary-syndrome.adverse: **Metformin** action causes nausea, cramps and **diarrhoea** while ovulation drugs risk multiple **pregnancy** and ovarian overresponse.

portal-hypertension.trigger: **Cirrhosis** with fibrosis and regenerative nodules distorts liver architecture and triggers raised resistance to blood flow through the **portal vein**.
portal-hypertension.target: Raised pressure acts on the **portal venous system**, **splanchnic circulation** and collateral veins linking the gut to the systemic circulation.
portal-hypertension.mechanism: Increased hepatic resistance plus increased splanchnic inflow raises **portal pressure**, opening **portosystemic collaterals** and driving fluid and blood into collateral beds.
portal-hypertension.manifestation: **Oesophageal varices** may bleed, **ascites** and **splenomegaly** develop, and gut derived toxins reaching the brain cause **hepatic encephalopathy**.
portal-hypertension.intervention: **Non selective beta blockers** lower portal inflow, **band ligation** obliterates varices, **lactulose** treats encephalopathy, and **TIPS** creates a shunt while diuretics treat ascites.
portal-hypertension.adverse: **Beta blockers** can cause **bradycardia**, hypotension and bronchospasm from beta blockade, while **TIPS** can worsen **hepatic encephalopathy** by bypassing liver detoxification.

postpartum-haemorrhage.trigger: Prolonged labour, overdistension, **retained placenta** or genital tract **trauma** leaves the **myometrium** unable to contract after birth.
postpartum-haemorrhage.target: The target is **myometrial fibres**, **spiral arteries** and the **clotting cascade** that must seal the placental bed.
postpartum-haemorrhage.mechanism: Without firm **uterine contraction**, open **spiral arteries** keep bleeding while retained **tissue** prevents closure of the placental bed.
postpartum-haemorrhage.manifestation: Atony causes a soft **boggy uterus** with steady **vaginal bleeding**, while trauma bleeds despite a firm uterus and coagulopathy causes persistent **oozing**.
postpartum-haemorrhage.intervention: **Uterine massage** plus **oxytocin** restores contraction and compresses vessels, while repair, tissue removal and **tranexamic acid** stop other causes.
postpartum-haemorrhage.adverse: **Oxytocin** can cause **hypotension** and fluid retention, while **tranexamic acid** can cause nausea and rare clot related harm.

pre-eclampsia.trigger: Abnormal early placentation with shallow **trophoblast** invasion leaves **spiral arteries** narrow and the placenta prone to ischaemia.
pre-eclampsia.target: The ischaemic placenta releases anti angiogenic factors such as **soluble fms like tyrosine kinase one** that injure maternal **vascular endothelium** widely.
pre-eclampsia.mechanism: Endothelial dysfunction causes vasoconstriction, **capillary leak** and platelet activation, reducing perfusion of **kidney**, liver, brain and placenta itself.
pre-eclampsia.manifestation: **Hypertension** with proteinuria reflects renal endothelial injury, while headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain and **eclampsia** signal cerebral and hepatic involvement.
pre-eclampsia.intervention: **Delivery** of the baby and placenta removes the cause, **magnesium sulphate** prevents seizures, and antihypertensive drugs control severe blood pressure.
pre-eclampsia.adverse: **Magnesium sulphate** can cause flushing, muscle weakness and respiratory depression from neuromuscular blockade, and rapid blood pressure lowering can compromise **placental perfusion**.

primary-hyperaldosteronism.trigger: An **adrenal adenoma** or bilateral **adrenal hyperplasia** secretes aldosterone unbidden. Autonomous release escapes normal **renin control** and drives the syndrome.
primary-hyperaldosteronism.target: **Mineralocorticoid receptors** in the **collecting duct** are the main target. Suppressed **juxtaglomerular cells** reflect the feedback from retained salt.
primary-hyperaldosteronism.mechanism: Excess **aldosterone action** inserts sodium channels that reclaim **sodium ions** and water. The exchange wastes **potassium ions** and hydrogen so alkalosis follows.
primary-hyperaldosteronism.manifestation: Salt and water retention causes resistant **hypertension** with headache and strain. Potassium and acid loss cause **muscle weakness** with cramps and **metabolic alkalosis**.
primary-hyperaldosteronism.intervention: **Spironolactone** blocks the receptor and reverses salt retention and potassium loss. Removing an **adrenal adenoma** by adrenalectomy cures unilateral disease durably.
primary-hyperaldosteronism.adverse: Blocking the receptor retains **potassium ions** toward **hyperkalaemia** with tingling and rhythm risk. **Spironolactone** also binds sex receptors causing breast tenderness and menstrual upset.

protein-synthesis-inhibitors.trigger: **Bacterial infection** with actively dividing organisms starts the process, as growth depends on continuous **protein synthesis** to make enzymes and structural proteins.
protein-synthesis-inhibitors.target: The target is the **bacterial ribosome**, where classes bind the **30S subunit** or the **50S subunit** at initiation, amino acid addition, or translocation.
protein-synthesis-inhibitors.mechanism: **Aminoglycosides** cause misreading at the **30S subunit**, while tetracyclines block tRNA entry and **macrolides** and related drugs block translocation or peptide transfer at the **50S subunit**.
protein-synthesis-inhibitors.manifestation: Blocked **protein synthesis** stops **bacterial growth** and colony expansion, so fever, pain, and tissue inflammation from the infection gradually settle as organisms are cleared.
protein-synthesis-inhibitors.intervention: **Aminoglycosides** and **tetracyclines** act at the 30S subunit, while chloramphenicol, macrolides, clindamycin, and **linezolid** act at the **50S subunit** to stop bacterial protein production.
protein-synthesis-inhibitors.adverse: **Aminoglycosides** can injure the **kidney** and **inner ear** through tissue accumulation, while chloramphenicol can suppress the **bone marrow** and macrolides can prolong cardiac repolarisation.

psoriasis-pathogenesis.trigger: **Genetic susceptibility** plus skin injury or infection triggers pathogenic **Th17 inflammation** in skin.
psoriasis-pathogenesis.target: **Dermal dendritic cells** and **keratinocytes** respond to **IL-17** and related cytokines in plaques.
psoriasis-pathogenesis.mechanism: **Dendritic cell signals** expand **Th17 cells** whose cytokines drive rapid **keratinocyte proliferation** and vessel growth.
psoriasis-pathogenesis.manifestation: **Scaly plaques** with **epidermal thickening** and redness reflect rapid turnover, with **psoriatic arthritis** when joints are involved.
psoriasis-pathogenesis.intervention: **Topical steroids** calm local inflammation, **phototherapy** slows turnover, and **biologics** block TNF, IL-17 or **IL-23 signalling**.
psoriasis-pathogenesis.adverse: **Topical steroids** thin **skin** and cause striae through collagen loss, while **biologics** raise infection risk by dampening immunity.

pulmonary-embolism.trigger: A **deep vein thrombosis** in a leg vein, promoted by **stasis**, vessel injury or hypercoagulability, provides the clot that embolises to the lungs.
pulmonary-embolism.target: The embolus lodges in a **pulmonary artery**, blocking blood flow to ventilated lung and straining the **right ventricle**.
pulmonary-embolism.mechanism: Blocked vessels create **dead space** with air but no blood, divert flow to other lung units and raise **pulmonary vascular resistance**. The right ventricle dilates against the sudden afterload.
pulmonary-embolism.manifestation: Sudden **breathlessness**, pleuritic pain and fast pulse with **hypoxaemia** follow, while large clots cause **right heart strain**, low blood pressure and collapse.
pulmonary-embolism.intervention: **Anticoagulants** stop clot growth and recurrence while the body breaks down existing clot. **Thrombolysis** or embolectomy is reserved for life threatening obstruction with circulatory collapse.
pulmonary-embolism.adverse: **Anticoagulants** impair **haemostasis** and cause bleeding from the gut, urinary tract or brain, especially after procedures or trauma. **Thrombolysis** greatly increases this bleeding risk.

pulmonary-hypertension.trigger: **Lung disease**, **chronic hypoxia** or an underlying cardiac or clot cause raises pulmonary vascular resistance.
pulmonary-hypertension.target: **Pulmonary arteries** and the **right ventricle** bear the pressure overload from increased resistance.
pulmonary-hypertension.mechanism: **Vasoconstriction** and vessel remodelling narrow the lumen so **right ventricular hypertrophy** progresses toward **right heart failure**.
pulmonary-hypertension.manifestation: **Breathlessness** and **fatigue** reflect poor output, with **raised jugular pressure** and ankle swelling as failure advances.
pulmonary-hypertension.intervention: **Oxygen**, **diuretics** and **pulmonary vasodilators** ease load, alongside treatment of the underlying cause.
pulmonary-hypertension.adverse: **Pulmonary vasodilators** can cause **systemic hypotension** and **headache** through unwanted systemic vessel relaxation.

pulmonary-oedema-mechanisms.trigger: Failing **left heart** with **fluid overload** starts cardiogenic flooding. Severe **sepsis** or lung injury starts permeability flooding by wounding the barrier.
pulmonary-oedema-mechanisms.target: The **alveolar capillary unit** with its thin **capillary endothelium** is the target. The **alveolar epithelium** plus interstitial space decide where fluid collects.
pulmonary-oedema-mechanisms.mechanism: Raised **hydrostatic pressure** or leaky **capillary permeability** pushes fluid by **Starling forces**. Fluid first widens the interstitium then floods **alveoli** and blocks gas exchange.
pulmonary-oedema-mechanisms.manifestation: Flooding causes severe **breathlessness** with crackles and falling **oxygen saturation**. Frothy **sputum** with fast breathing marks alveolar filling that explains urgent support.
pulmonary-oedema-mechanisms.intervention: **Diuretic and nitrate** therapy lowers preload and clears cardiogenic fluid. **Positive pressure support** recruits flooded alveoli while treating the **underlying cause** stops recurrence.
pulmonary-oedema-mechanisms.adverse: Strong **diuretic and nitrate** action can drop pressure into **hypotension** with dizziness. Positive pressure can dry airway and cause **mask discomfort** that limits tolerance.

raas.trigger: Falling renal perfusion, salt delivery or sympathetic drive stimulates **renin** release from the **juxtaglomerular apparatus**.
raas.target: Renin starts a cascade through **angiotensinogen**, **angiotensin converting enzyme** and the **AT1 receptor**, ending with aldosterone release.
raas.mechanism: **Renin** forms angiotensin I, **ACE** converts it to angiotensin II, and **AT1 receptor** activation constricts vessels and releases aldosterone. Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption in the collecting duct.
raas.manifestation: Sustained activation raises blood pressure and volume and promotes cardiac and vascular remodelling. It worsens **heart failure** and **proteinuric kidney disease** despite sometimes normal blood pressure.
raas.intervention: **ACE inhibitors** and **angiotensin receptor blockers** reduce angiotensin II signalling. **Aldosterone antagonists** block the mineralocorticoid receptor, and **aliskiren** inhibits renin directly.
raas.adverse: **ACE inhibitors** allow **bradykinin** to accumulate, causing cough and angioedema. All effective blockade can cause hypotension, rising creatinine and **hyperkalaemia**, especially with kidney disease.

rabies-neural-spread.trigger: Bite inoculation of **rabies virus** in saliva into **muscle tissue** and skin **wounds**, with delayed **wound washing**.
rabies-neural-spread.target: Virus enters peripheral **motor neurons** and travels by retrograde **axonal transport** toward the **spinal cord** and **brain**.
rabies-neural-spread.mechanism: Virus replicates in **neuronal cytoplasm** and spreads across **synapses** to the brain, causing diffuse **encephalitis** and spread to **salivary glands**.
rabies-neural-spread.manifestation: Encephalitis produces agitation with **hydrophobia** and **aerophobia**, while autonomic storm and **paralysis** progress to coma and fatal **respiratory failure**.
rabies-neural-spread.intervention: Thorough **wound washing** removes virus while timely **vaccine** plus **immunoglobulin** builds neutralising **antibodies** before nerve entry.
rabies-neural-spread.adverse: **Vaccine** and **immunoglobulin** can cause injection site **pain** with fever and **headache** from immune activation, which usually settles with rest.

raised-icp.trigger: A mass, bleeding, tumour or brain swelling adds volume inside the rigid skull and triggers raised **intracranial pressure** under the **Monro Kellie doctrine** once compensation fails.
raised-icp.target: Pressure affects **brain tissue**, **cerebral blood vessels** and **cerebrospinal fluid** spaces within the fixed cranial vault.
raised-icp.mechanism: Early displacement of cerebrospinal fluid and venous blood preserves pressure, but further volume exhausts **compliance** and pressure rises steeply. Falling **cerebral perfusion pressure** causes ischaemia and tissue shifts toward **herniation**.
raised-icp.manifestation: Headache, vomiting, reduced consciousness and **papilledema** develop, with pupil changes and posturing as herniation progresses. The **Cushing response** gives rising blood pressure, slow pulse and irregular breathing.
raised-icp.intervention: **Head elevation** aids venous drainage, **osmotherapy** draws water from brain tissue, **cerebrospinal fluid drainage** removes volume, and **decompression** creates space when other measures fail.
raised-icp.adverse: **Mannitol** can cause dehydration and kidney injury from **osmotic diuresis**, while **cerebrospinal fluid drainage** carries infection, bleeding and overdrainage risk.

renal-filtration-gfr.trigger: Changes in **arterial pressure** and **sodium chloride** delivery to the **macula densa** demand adjustment of glomerular filtration.
renal-filtration-gfr.target: **Afferent arteriole**, **efferent arteriole** and the **glomerular filtration barrier** set glomerular pressure and filtration.
renal-filtration-gfr.mechanism: Afferent dilatation or efferent constriction raises **glomerular capillary pressure**, while **tubuloglomerular feedback** and autoregulation stabilise **filtration rate** despite pressure change.
renal-filtration-gfr.manifestation: Falling filtration reduces **urine output** and causes retention of **creatinine** and potassium, while excessive filtration pressure injures the **glomerulus** over time.
renal-filtration-gfr.intervention: An **NSAID** blocks protective **prostaglandins** and constricts the afferent arteriole, whereas an **ACE inhibitor** reduces angiotensin effect and dilates the efferent arteriole.
renal-filtration-gfr.adverse: Both drug classes can lower **glomerular pressure** enough to cause acute fall in **filtration rate**, and ACE inhibition also promotes **hyperkalaemia**.

renal-osteodystrophy-ckd-mbd.trigger: Progressive **CKD** with falling filtration retains **phosphate** and lowers active **vitamin D** synthesis. The defect begins in failing **renal** tissue.
renal-osteodystrophy-ckd-mbd.target: Targets are the **parathyroid glands**, bone remodelling units and renal **phosphate** handling. Low calcium with high phosphate jointly stimulates **PTH** release.
renal-osteodystrophy-ckd-mbd.mechanism: Low **calcium** with high **phosphate** and low vitamin D drives excess **PTH** release. The hormone activates **osteoclasts**, which resorb bone and weaken structure.
renal-osteodystrophy-ckd-mbd.manifestation: Chronic **PTH** excess causes **bone pain**, **fractures** and deformity from high turnover loss. Vascular calcification with **pruritus** reflects disturbed mineral balance.
renal-osteodystrophy-ckd-mbd.intervention: **Phosphate binder** drugs trap dietary **phosphate** in the gut and lower its load. **Calcimimetic** therapy sensitises the parathyroid **calcium sensing receptor** and lowers hormone release.
renal-osteodystrophy-ckd-mbd.adverse: **Calcium based binders** can raise **calcium** and promote vascular calcification through positive balance. **Calcimimetic** drugs may cause **hypocalcaemia** with nausea through receptor overactivation.

renal-tubular-acidosis.trigger: Inherited or acquired **tubular defects**, or reduced **aldosterone** action, prevent the kidney reclaiming bicarbonate or secreting acid normally.
renal-tubular-acidosis.target: The **proximal tubule** normally reclaims filtered bicarbonate, while the **distal tubule** and **collecting duct** secrete hydrogen ions into urine.
renal-tubular-acidosis.mechanism: Proximal failure wastes **bicarbonate**, distal failure traps acid and promotes **stones**, and low aldosterone action impairs acid and **potassium** excretion.
renal-tubular-acidosis.manifestation: All types cause hyperchloraemic **metabolic acidosis** with growth failure in children, while distal disease adds **nephrocalcinosis** and the hypoaldosteronism type adds **hyperkalaemia**.
renal-tubular-acidosis.intervention: **Bicarbonate** replaces lost alkali, **potassium** corrects distal depletion, and a **mineralocorticoid** restores distal excretion when aldosterone action is deficient.
renal-tubular-acidosis.adverse: Excess **bicarbonate** can cause sodium and volume overload, **potassium** supplements risk hyperkalaemia, and **mineralocorticoids** can cause hypertension and oedema.

reproductive-axis-drugs.trigger: **Infertility**, endometriosis, prostate cancer or assisted reproduction creates a need to stimulate or suppress the **reproductive axis** in a controlled way.
reproductive-axis-drugs.target: Drugs act at hypothalamic **oestrogen receptors**, pituitary **GnRH receptors**, or gonadal LH and FSH receptors reached by injected gonadotropins.
reproductive-axis-drugs.mechanism: Pulsatile GnRH restores **LH** and **FSH** release, continuous agonist first flares then desensitises the pituitary, antagonists block at once, and clomiphene removes **oestrogen feedback**.
reproductive-axis-drugs.manifestation: Stimulation produces follicle growth, **ovulation** or testosterone production, while suppression lowers sex hormones and shrinks hormone dependent tissue but causes **hot flushes**.
reproductive-axis-drugs.intervention: **Clomiphene** induces ovulation, **GnRH antagonists** prevent premature ovulation, continuous GnRH agonists suppress sex hormones, and **FSH** with **hCG** directly stimulate gonads.
reproductive-axis-drugs.adverse: Stimulation can cause **ovarian hyperstimulation** and multiple pregnancy, clomiphene causes **visual symptoms** and flushes, and suppression causes bone loss and **sexual dysfunction**.

respiratory-failure-types.trigger: Lung injury from **pneumonia** or fluid impairs gas exchange, while weak **drive** or tired **respiratory muscles** impair pumping.
respiratory-failure-types.target: Targets are **alveoli**, pulmonary **capillaries** and the pump of brainstem drive, nerves, **diaphragm** and chest wall.
respiratory-failure-types.mechanism: Mismatch and **shunt** let blood pass without oxygen in type one failure, while weak pumping lets **carbon dioxide** rise in type two **ventilatory failure**.
respiratory-failure-types.manifestation: Type one causes low **oxygen levels** with breathlessness, type two adds rising **carbon dioxide**, drowsiness and **acidosis** from poor ventilation.
respiratory-failure-types.intervention: **Oxygen** corrects low oxygen, **noninvasive ventilation** rests muscles and clears carbon dioxide, and **invasive ventilation** takes over severe failure.
respiratory-failure-types.adverse: **Oxygen** can worsen carbon dioxide retention in at risk lungs, while **ventilation** can injure **airways** and lower blood pressure.

respiratory-mechanics.trigger: Contraction of the **diaphragm** and **external intercostal muscles** creates the demand for inspiratory airflow.
respiratory-mechanics.target: **Pleural pressure**, alveolar elastic recoil and **airway resistance** determine lung expansion and flow.
respiratory-mechanics.mechanism: Falling pleural pressure expands alveoli, **surfactant** reduces **surface tension**, and the resulting pressure gradient drives air inward until recoil balances expansion.
respiratory-mechanics.manifestation: Stiff lungs give a **restrictive pattern** with small volumes, while narrowed airways give an **obstructive pattern** with prolonged expiration and **air trapping**.
respiratory-mechanics.intervention: A **bronchodilator** relaxes airway smooth muscle and lowers resistance, while exogenous **surfactant** improves compliance in surfactant deficient lungs.
respiratory-mechanics.adverse: A **bronchodilator** acting on **beta receptors** can also cause tremor, palpitations and tachycardia from systemic receptor stimulation.

rheumatic-fever.trigger: Untreated **group A streptococcal** throat infection triggers an aberrant **immune response** in a susceptible host after a latent interval.
rheumatic-fever.target: Antibodies and T cells against streptococcal **M protein** cross react with **cardiac myosin**, joint, skin and brain antigens by molecular mimicry.
rheumatic-fever.mechanism: Cross reactive immunity causes inflammation of heart valves and myocardium, migratory **synovitis**, basal ganglia dysfunction and skin lesions, with **valve scarring** after repeated attacks.
rheumatic-fever.manifestation: The **Jones features** are carditis, migratory arthritis, **Sydenham chorea**, subcutaneous nodules and erythema marginatum, and chronic disease causes progressive valve stenosis or regurgitation.
rheumatic-fever.intervention: **Penicillin** eradicates streptococci, **anti inflammatory drugs** control arthritis and carditis symptoms, and long term secondary prophylaxis prevents recurrent attacks.
rheumatic-fever.adverse: **Penicillin** can cause allergy and anaphylaxis, **aspirin** and other anti inflammatory drugs can cause gastric injury, and missed prophylaxis allows damaging recurrence.

rheumatoid-arthritis.trigger: Loss of tolerance in a genetically susceptible host lets **autoreactive T cells** and **B cells** target joint antigens. Environmental stress on the **synovium** sustains the autoimmune response.
rheumatoid-arthritis.target: Activated immune cells release **tumour necrosis factor** and **interleukin** that act on **synovial fibroblasts** and endothelium. The inflamed synovium thickens into invasive tissue.
rheumatoid-arthritis.mechanism: **Cytokines** recruit leukocytes and drive synovial proliferation, forming **pannus** over cartilage. Pannus and **osteoclasts** activated by inflammatory signals erode cartilage and subchondral bone.
rheumatoid-arthritis.manifestation: Symmetrical painful swelling of small joints with **morning stiffness** reflects active **synovitis**. Progressive deformity, erosions on imaging and raised inflammatory markers reflect cartilage loss and bone erosion.
rheumatoid-arthritis.intervention: **Methotrexate** and other DMARDs suppress immune activation, while **TNF blockers** neutralise tumour necrosis factor. **Glucocorticoids** give rapid relief by broadly suppressing cytokine transcription.
rheumatoid-arthritis.adverse: **Methotrexate** can cause marrow suppression and liver injury from its antifolate action. **TNF blockers** increase infection risk, and **glucocorticoids** cause hyperglycaemia, osteoporosis and adrenal suppression.

rickets-vitamin-d-deficiency.trigger: Low **sunlight exposure** plus poor dietary **vitamin D** and **calcium intake** starts deficiency. Malabsorption or chronic kidney disease adds to the defect.
rickets-vitamin-d-deficiency.target: The **gut epithelium** for calcium uptake, the **kidney** for final activation, and the **growth plate** with **osteoid** for mineralisation are targets.
rickets-vitamin-d-deficiency.mechanism: Low active **calcitriol** reduces intestinal **calcium absorption** and renal **phosphate reabsorption**. Rising **parathyroid hormone** then pulls mineral from bone while osteoid stays soft.
rickets-vitamin-d-deficiency.manifestation: Soft **growth plate** widens and bows under weight causing **bowed legs** and **rachitic rosary**. Children show bone pain, delayed growth and muscle weakness.
rickets-vitamin-d-deficiency.intervention: **Vitamin D** with **calcium supplements** plus safe **sunlight exposure** restores mineral supply for healing. Surgery corrects fixed deformity once bones remineralise.
rickets-vitamin-d-deficiency.adverse: Excess **vitamin D** drives **hypercalcaemia** with thirst, polyuria and confusion from overabsorption. Extra **calcium salts** add constipation and kidney stones from urinary load.

salicylate-poisoning.trigger: Excess **aspirin** ingestion for pain or deliberate **overdose** delivers more **salicylate** than liver and kidney can clear.
salicylate-poisoning.target: Targets are the medullary **respiratory centre**, mitochondrial **oxidative phosphorylation** and renal **tubular excretion** of weak acid.
salicylate-poisoning.mechanism: Direct centre stimulation causes **hyperventilation** while uncoupling wastes energy as **heat**, generating **lactic acid** and keto acids with dehydration.
salicylate-poisoning.manifestation: **Tachypnoea** with **tinnitus** and sweating progresses to confusion, **hyperthermia** and **acidotic breathing** with worsening consciousness.
salicylate-poisoning.intervention: **Activated charcoal** limits absorption while **urinary alkalinisation** traps ionised drug in urine and **dialysis** removes severe load.
salicylate-poisoning.adverse: **Bicarbonate** therapy can cause **hypokalaemia** and fluid overload while **dialysis** risks **hypotension** from rapid shifts.

sarcoidosis.trigger: **Unknown antigen** in a susceptible host starts an exaggerated **CD4 T cell** response in lung and nodes.
sarcoidosis.target: **Alveolar macrophages** and **CD4 T cells** around arterioles and lymphatics organise into granulomas.
sarcoidosis.mechanism: **Activated macrophages** fuse into **multinucleated giant cells** forming **non-caseating granulomas** that may fibrose.
sarcoidosis.manifestation: **Hilar lymphadenopathy** and **breathlessness** mark lung disease, with **uveitis** and heart block showing other organ spread.
sarcoidosis.intervention: **Corticosteroids** suppress granuloma inflammation and **immunosuppressants** are added when disease is severe or persistent.
sarcoidosis.adverse: **Corticosteroids** raise **blood glucose** and weaken **bone strength** through metabolic and bone turnover effects.

schizophrenia-dopamine-pathways.trigger: Neurodevelopmental vulnerability plus **stress** and **cannabis** exposure destabilises **dopamine** signalling in adolescent brain circuits.
schizophrenia-dopamine-pathways.target: Targets are **D2 receptors** on striatal and pituitary cells plus the **mesolimbic**, **mesocortical** and **nigrostriatal** pathways.
schizophrenia-dopamine-pathways.mechanism: Excess **mesolimbic** drive overstimulates **D2 receptors** while weak **mesocortical** drive impairs cognition, and blockade restores balance but also silences motor and hormonal control.
schizophrenia-dopamine-pathways.manifestation: **Hallucinations** and **delusions** reflect mesolimbic excess while flat affect and **avolition** reflect cortical deficit, and overblockade adds stiffness and **galactorrhoea**.
schizophrenia-dopamine-pathways.intervention: **Typical antipsychotics** strongly block **D2 receptors** while **atypical antipsychotics** combine weaker D2 blockade with **5HT2A** antagonism for broader control.
schizophrenia-dopamine-pathways.adverse: **D2 blockade** in motor circuits causes **parkinsonism** and **tardive dyskinesia** while pituitary blockade raises **prolactin** with metabolic effects from broader action.

screening-test-2x2-table.trigger: Hidden **disease cases** in a population create need for early detection. A simple **screening test** with a clear cut off meets that demand.
screening-test-2x2-table.target: The ill **disease group**, the healthy **non disease group** and the chosen **test cut off** that splits results are the targets.
